useLimitation.gco:CharacterString: The data is intended for use as a tool for display and general GIS analysis purposes only. It is in no way intended for engineering or legal purposes. The data accuracy is checked against best available sources which may be dated. NPS assumes no liability for use of this data. Boundaries with the word "Lands" starting the GIS_NOTES attribute have completed the Land Resources Program entire QA/QC processes. Boundaries that begin with the word "Preliminary" in the GIS_NOTES field, while generally created using the same methods as the "Lands" boundaries, have not completed the entire QA/QC process as should be treated as preliminary data only. Boundaries from the Land Resources Program will have separate polygons for each type of unit designation. For example, Denali National Park and Denali National Preserve are separate individual polygons. This data is updated quarterly.

Property ownership data is compiled from deeds, plats, surveys, and other source data. These are not engineering quality drawings and should be used for administrative purposes only. The National Park Service shall not be held liable for improper or incorrect use of the data described and/or contained herein. These data and related graphics are not legal documents and are not intended to be used as such. The information contained in these data is dynamic and may change over time. The data are not better than the original sources from which they were derived. It is the responsibility of the data user to use the data appropriately and consistent within the limitations of geospatial data in general and these data in particular. The related graphics are intended to aid the data user in acquiring relevant data; it is not appropriate to use the related graphics as data. The National Park Service gives no warranty, expressed or implied, as to the accuracy, reliability, or completeness of these data. It is strongly recommended that these data are directly acquired from an NPS server and not indirectly through other sources which may have changed the data in some way. Although these data have been processed successfully on a computer system at the National Park Service, no warranty expressed or implied is made regarding the utility of the data on another system or for general or scientific purposes, nor shall the act of distribution constitute any such warranty. This disclaimer applies both to individual use of the data and aggregate use with other data.

description.gco:CharacterString: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 10/03/2007 Line work was digitized from the original Mylar Land Status Map of the Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historic Site in 2002, using AutoCAD Land Development Desktop (LDD) by Avineon, Inc., 4825 Mark Center Drive, Suite 700, Alexandria VA 22311-1846. POC: Xiaodong Hong, Manager, Geographic Information Systems, (703) 671-1900. Email: xhong@avineon.com. Digitized line work was then verified by the SER Office personnel from deeds, legal descriptions, and survey data (when available). Map Projection is Kentucky State Plane, NAD27, US foot . When discrepancies were identified, individual tracts were re-plotted by use of COGO, using AutoCAD LDD. Data was geo-referenced to DOQQ, Kentucky State Plane, NAD 83. Topology was created for park boundary and individual tracts. Primary validation of cartographic attributes was verified by displaying the lines in both database and the spatial coverage, but no formal tests were performed. Database attributes were linked during the topology creation process. Database attributes were retrieved from the National Park Service, Management Information System, Master Deeds List (MIS/MDL). Clean Topology was developed and attributes were assigned in AutoCad Map using the Drawing Clean-up function at a tolerance level of 0.10 and Object Data links. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Agate Fossil Beds National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 11/27/2012 The AutoDesk project was projected to Nebraska State Plane, NAD83, US Feet. PLSS line work from the BLM’s Geocommunicator site appeared to be the best source for Township-Range information. PLSS was downloaded from http://www.geocommunicator.gov/GeoComm/index.shtm on 20091117. However this data has many spatial errors. The legal descriptions for tracts 01-104, 01-105, 01-105A&B, 01-115 and 01-127 were transformed around the SW corner of section 12 (X = 642056.80, Y = 959570.84) and the approximate intersection of the center line of the 33’ right-of-way (01-127) and southerly right-of-way line of county road 258 (X = 638159.49, Y = 969253.51) to account for ground to grid translation. Used the MATCH command in AutoCAD’s Raster Design to geo-reference, scale and rotate the boundary survey for AGFO (http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/agfo/Miscellaneous_Maps/agfo1653007-001.pdf) using the NW corner of section 6 (X = 616035.82, Y = 970787.22) and the intersection of the SE corner of tract 01-109 and the NW corner of tract 01-105B (X = 636065.46, Y = 964959.49) to account for ground to grid translation. Boundary and internal section lines (3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10) were on-screen digitized from image of boundary survey. All other section lines were taken from BLM PLSS line work. The county road center line used to create tract 01-103 was on-screen digitized from 2009 NAIP. A 40’ right-of-way was assumed fro tract 01-103. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step. Changed the attribute of tract 01-105B to 01-105A.

description.gco:CharacterString: Alagnak Wild River Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/21/2019 In 1993, the ALAG hand-drawn mylar Lands segment sheet was created. It was continually revised as needed until 2002. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Alagnak Wild River segment map by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. Other digital sources used in the initial digital data set included: best available hydrography and digital public lands survey system maps. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside of the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tract coverages. Attribute and linework errors were resolved, better digital sources were used (DOQQs, survey data, revised USGS hydrography, PLSS, etc.), and land status changes were updated. From 2002 to 2009, many boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the AKRO Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, cogoing the U.S., M.S., BLM, and NPS surveys, using the written legal descriptions for the park boundaries, using private and federal deed descriptions/plats, NOAA-surveyed shorelines, and using a contract-produced (RDI, Inc.) year 2000 aerial photo mosaic to digitize shorelines, etc. All work done was converted into ArcInfo files, attributed, and submitted each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team, and specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. In 2008-2009, the Cobell restrictions on restricted use of Native Allotment data was lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. All ALAG tracts have been cogoed from the U.S. Surveys and the land status including native allotments is current as of May 5, 2009. Tract and boundary data is continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude. State tracts were created for the following navigable waters: Alagnak River, Nonvianuk River, Kukaklek Lake, and Nonvianuk Lake. The 2000 Alagnak River Corridor Photo Mosaic was used for the bulk of the shoreline digitizing. A Riparian Specialist with the BLM were consulted for mapping the tract shoreline at the estimated Ordinary High Water Mark (OHWM). A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets. In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Allegheny Portage Railroad National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 06/03/2014 The park boundary and individual tract boundaries were drawn utilizing cogo commands in Autodesk based on the bearing and distance legal descriptions found in deeds and surveys provided here http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/ALPO/. Tracts that were cogod from deeds located at the aforementioned site were 101-01, 101-04, 101-06, 101-07, 101-08, 101-09, 101-17, 102-03, 102-05, 102-06, 102-07, 102-12, 102-15, 102-16, 102-20, 102-21, 102-25, 102-29, 102-30, 102-36, 102-37, 102-39, 103-01, 103-02, 103-03, 103-04, 103-06, 104-01, 104-02, 104-04, 105-01, 105-02, 105-03, 105-04, 105-05, 105-06, 105-07, 105-08, 105-09,105-10,105-11, 105-12, 105-13,105-14,105-17,105-18,105-105-19,105-22 and 105-23. County generated boundary and tract line work were changed to match the legal descriptions reflected by the cogo’ed tracts listed above. Tract 103-01 was rotated 4d14’44”. Tract 103-03 was rotated 357d4’40”. Tract 104-1 was rotated 3d43’5”. Tract 105-13 was rotated 357d0’22”. Tract 105-16 was rotated 332d7’8”. Tract 105-11 was rotated 2d37’23”. Tracts 101-03, 104-04 and 105-23 had portions of their boundary cogo’ed and portions of their boundary derived from county data. Tracts 102-04, 102-05, and 102-37 boundaries were derived from tracts adjoining that were cogo’ed. Tracts 102-08, 102-11, 102-10, 102-29, 102-28, 102-27, 102-29, 102-26, 102-30, 102-32, 102-24, 102-23, 102-13, 102-14, 102-15, 102-16, 102-17, 102-18, 102-19, 102-20, 102-22, 102-21, 102-12, 102-43, 102-02, 102-01, 103-06, 103-07, 104-07, 105-07, 105-08, 105-09, 105-03, 105-19, and 106-04 were generated by first using the available Cambria or Blair County GIS data. If the County data was unavailable on screen digitization was performed using legacy segment maps that are located here http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/ALPO/Segment_Maps. Also, the imagery used for the onscreen digitization process was 2011 Digital Ortho Quads downloaded from the following USDA website http://datagateway.nrcs.usda.gov/. The remaining tracts not mentioned above were copied over from the county parcel data due to lack information present. There is a known acreage discrepancy for tracts 102-20, 102-30, 103-01, and 103-03. This was discovered after comparing the cogo’ed tract acreage and the acreage listed in the respective deeds. Lands always upholds the deeded acreage unless there is a legally more accurate account of a tracts acreage such as a new deed, updated survey, ect. NAD83 Pennsylvania South Central State Planes, US Foot was used as the source coordinate system for the Autodesk Land Desktop project. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then re-projected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step. UPDATE: 12/18/2023 Update 12/18/2023. Updated tract and boundary data for entire park unit utilizing exterior boundary survey point data provided by park staff and 2020 CAD data provided by an NPS contract surveyor for a portion of the Summit Area (segment 102). Survey point data was confirmed with line data input using the GIS Pro Traverse tool and bearing and distance information from various land survey plats: 2023 Minor Sub/Lot Combination, TCF/Miller, Inst. No. 202313658, Bk. 124, Pg. 48 (Blair County); 2007 Survey of Tract 106-04 (unrecorded); 1996 Cresson Center Property Survey, NPS Drawing No. 423-149199; 1975 Linderman Plat Map (no doc. number); 1984 Boundary Survey, NPS Drawing No. 423-41019; 1989 Boundary Survey, NPS Drawing No. 423-41027; 1994 Boundary Survey, NPS Drawing No. 423-41037; 1996 Boundary Survey, NPS Drawing No. 423-41019A, 2016 Cresson Center Final Subdivision, Cambria County File No. 2016-00001420; 2019 Linderman Tract Subdivision Plan, Blair County File No. 2019-4464-001; 2020 NPS contracted Partial Boundary Survey, Summit area (no doc. number); and PA DOT Hwy ROW Map, NPS Drawing No. 423-149068. After the exterior legislated boundary was completed, the interior tract (parcel) boundaries were created using the same GIS tool from recorded deed descriptions. Tracts without exterior boundary survey points were adjusted to georeferenced aerial photography utilizing apparent boundary line features (railroad ROW extents, creek/river beds, road ROWs, fencing, etc.).

description.gco:CharacterString: Amistad National Recreation Area UPDATE: 08/26/2024 Tract and boundary data updated per 9/21/2023 BLM original survey - Amistad National Recreation Area, Block A, Sections 17 and 18, Val Verde County, TX. UPDATE: 12/14/2023 Tract and boundary data updated per the following surveys: August 2021 by Bohannan Huston - Boundary Survey of Amistad National Recreation Area, Pink Cave Cove; August 2021 by Bohannan Huston - Boundary Survey of Amistad National Recreation Area, Pump Canyon Tributary UPDATE: 07/22/2019 Creation: Data is based on various sources, including land surveys and where applicable, contours derived from LiDAR data. The majority of the boundary of Amistad follows the 1144.3 ft contour (NGVD27). The total boundary length is approximately 600 miles. Of this total, approximately 115 miles has been surveyed. The remaining boundary work was COGO'd from surveys of record, International Boundary Water Commission (IBWC) acquisition documents and contour data produced from 2017 LiDAR data prepared for USGS/NGTOC (Job No. PAR-0140-002, USGS Contract No. G17PC00007). Once tract line topology is checked, tract and boundary polygon topology are created. Sources for tract boundary work include IBWC acquisition maps, deeds and easement grant documents, survey and subdivision plats, and public right-of-way plan sets. Park tract boundaries are intended to represent legal property boundaries. Once the tract polygons are created, this layer is exported for use with AutoCAD or reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude for posting to the IRMA portal. Topology rules and are developed for both the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5.

It was continually revised as needed until 2003. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Aniakchak National Monument and Preserve segment map by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. Other digital sources used in the initial digital data set included: best available hydrography and digital public lands survey system maps. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside of the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tract coverages. Attribute and linework errors were resolved, better digital sources were used (DOQQs, survey data, revised USGS hydrography, PLSS, etc.), and land status changes were updated. From 2002 to 2009, many boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the AKRO Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, cogoing the U.S., M.S., BLM, and NPS surveys, using the written legal descriptions for the park boundaries, using private and federal deed descriptions/plats, NOAA-surveyed shorelines, and using better orthophoto/DRG data to digitize shorelines, ridge boundaries, etc. During this time, some boundary linework (with Lands review) was also created by AKRO GIS specialist(s). Encompass converted the data into ArcInfo files, attributed it, and submitted the data each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). During 2008, the common boundary with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's Alaska Peninsula Refuge was minorly revised and agreed upon by both agencies. In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team, and specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Also in 2009, the selected native corporation lands were substantially reduced because they had overselected the amount of lands they will actually be able to receive under ANCSA regulations. Hence, they "prioritized" their selections; most of these lands will likely go to patent during 2009+. In 2008-2009, the Cobell restrictions on gov't. use of Native Allotment data were lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. The two small tracts in ANIA have only a digitized location/boundary and need to be cogoed as of May 14, 2009. The shoreline is also in need of a better dataset- not available at this time (May 14, 2009). Tract and boundary data is continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude and longitude. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

The Autodesk line work was imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology was developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5 revised 2017. The entire unit was created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data was then exported from Autodesk to an ESRI shapeﬁle format and reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude by the Lands Fort Collins Oﬃce. Since this data was created, edits have been made to the original shapeﬁle using Autodesk Civil 3D, ArcGIS Map, and ArcGIS Pro using appropriate local coordinate systems. This data is exported from these environments in either a shapeﬁle or geodatabase format using a North American Datum 1983 projection.

description.gco:CharacterString: Bering Land Bridge National Preserve Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/21/2019 In October 1994, the BELA hand-drawn mylar Land Resources Division segment sheets were created. They were continually revised as needed until 2002. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Bering Land Bridge National Preserve segment maps by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. using ESRI software in the form of coverages, and, under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. Other digital sources used in the initial digital data set included: best available hydrography and digital public lands survey system maps. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside of the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS and using ESRI software in the form of coverages, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tracts. Attribute and linework errors were resolved, better digital sources were used (DOQQs, survey data, revised USGS hydrography, PLSS, etc.), and land status changes were updated. From 2002 to 2009, many boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the Alaska Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, cogoing the U.S., M.S., BLM, and NPS surveys using survey and Autodesk software, using the written legal descriptions for the park boundaries, using private and federal deed descriptions/plats, NOAA-surveyed shorelines, and using better orthophoto/DRG data to digitize shorelines, ridge boundaries, etc. The BELA marine shoreline was revised in 2007 using accurate NOAA Mean High Water linework created from 2003 NOAA LIDAR and hydrographic survey techniques. During this time, some boundary linework (with Lands review) was also created by AKRO GIS specialist(s). NPS administrative parcels outside of the park were mapped by Lands during 2007-2008. Encompass converted the data into ArcInfo files, attributed it, and submitted the data each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase created under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team. Specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Also in 2009, the selected native corporation lands were substantially reduced because they had overselected the amount of lands they will actually be able to receive under ANCSA regulations. Hence, the regional and village corporations "prioritized" their selections- most of these lands will likely go to patent during 2009+ (Kikitagruk, Inc. I.C.'d their lands in late 2008, Ahtna will likely do the same in 2009). In 2008, the Cobell restrictions on gov't. use of Native Allotment data were lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. In progress 2009, many of the native allotments are being cogoed-in by Lands Cartographers. 2008-produced BLM digital cogoed native allotments and other U.S. Surveys are also being incorporated into the NPS lands system after comparing to NPS cogo work or other maps. Any portions of the BELA park boundary having a common boundary with the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service are being agreed upon (in-progress during 2009-2010). Tract and boundary data is continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude and longitude. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Boston Harbor Islands National Recreation Area Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 11/23/2022 Nautical charts are updated as part of an ongoing process to create a cartographic representation of the best available data collected through the years employing a variety of data collection technology and techniques and provided to the Office of Coast Survey using numerous different scales, datums, and projections. Technology has allowed for a drastic increase in positional accuracy. However, historical data has not been superseded in many areas. The availability of digital chart products and Differential Global Positioning System (DGPS) has drastically changed navigation. Navigation systems using DGPS for locating a vessel's position on the earth have put mariners in a unique predicament due to a false perception of greater positional accuracy of features portrayed on the charts. In many cases, the DGPS is more accurate than the surveying technology that was used to put the soundings and features on the nautical chart, paper or raster. The data accuracy is checked against its source nautical chart only. NOAA assumes no liability for use of this data. The data accuracy is checked against its source nautical chart only. Nautical charts are verified and updated as part of an ongoing process to create a cartographic representation of the best available data collected through the years employing a variety of collection techniques and provided to the Office of Coast Survey using numerous different data types, scales, datums, and projections. Prior to 1995, the paper charts were composed manually. In 1995, the paper charts were scanned to create the raster charts. Both the paper and raster charts are composed from the same digital files. The data accuracy is checked against its source nautical chart only. NOAA assumes no liability for use of this data. The NOAA Nautical Chart Manual Seventh (1992) Edition contains a complete list of selection criteria, generalization, and definitions that were used to determine what is included in the data set. Charting material consists principally of topographic and hydrographic surveys made by NOS supplemented by miscellaneous surveys and textual information provided by other organizations. All material must be critically examined, with particular attention directed to the actual date of the survey, geographic datum, depth unit, plane of reference, purpose and quality of the survey, and whether it is an original source or from another compilation. A partial listing of sources of cartographic data follows: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, U.S. Coast Guard, National Imagery and Mapping Agency, NOAA Office of Coast Survey/National Ocean Service, U.S. Geological Survey, St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corp, Environmental Protection Agency, U.S. National Park Service, State Department, NOAA National Weather Service, NOAA National Marine Fisheries, National Archives, NOAA National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service, state and local sources, private sources, and international sources. The data is intended for use as an imagery backdrop to represent the charted hydrography and topography of a given area. It is in no way intended for navigational uses. The data accuracy is checked against its source nautical chart only. NOAA assumes no liability for use of this data. The vector shoreline data were originally derived from NOAA Nautical Charts using a process and software developed by the Coast Survey Development Laboratory, Cartographic & Geospatial Technology Program (CGTP). The products' target scale of 1:20,000 allows for applications at a higher spatial resolution that was not possible with the prior 1:80,000 digital shoreline. The derived vector shoreline data are provided in the shapefile format used in GIS (Geographic Information Systems) environments. Vector shoreline data are intended for GIS applications. The derived Mean High Water and Mean Lower Low Water outlines may not always correspond to these well-defined shoreline datums. The derived vector data are not intended to be used for navigation nor to be interpreted as the legal shoreline. Data accuracy is checked against the source nautical charts. NOAA assumes no liability for use of these data. Vector shoreline data were originally derived from NOAA nautical charts using a process and software developed by CGTP. The derived Mean High Water and Mean Lower Low Water outlines were originally processed from the 762 dpi binary raster files that are used to produce nautical charts. The derived shoreline data were converted from paper-charted units to geographic coordinates, then imported to ESRI shapefile (vector) format. Once the data was brought into the DWG, the line work was selected and copied to either the boundary layer. Tract 020-101 was COGO'd from a legal description. Topology was then successfully built and exported to an ESRI shapefile. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native coordinate system of the DWG is Massachusetts State Plane Zone Islands, NAD83, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Canyon de Chelly National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 11/03/2015 BLM GCDB was used for the PLSS portion of the CACH boundary, being the most westerly portion. For the rest of the boundary, USGS SDTS data was converted to DLG and imported into Autodesk. The DLG data was placed on top of USDA NAIP and the canyon rim contour was copied and exported to ArcView, where a half mile buffer was placed around the canyon rim. PLSS line work was then joined with the DLG data to create a boundary for the park. The line work was then copied to the appropriate layer (BDY-NPS). The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step. Source drawing coordinate system was Arizona State Plane Coordinate System, East Zone, NAD 83, US Foot. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The positional accuracy of this dataset is dependent upon the scales of the maps which this dataset is drawn from. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy.

description.gco:CharacterString: Canyonlands National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 04/22/2010 BLM GDBC digital flat files were downloaded on 01/14/2010 from http://www.blm.gov/wo/st/en/prog/more/gcdb.html for the area that encompasses CANY. This line work was used to create all aliquot part tracts as shown on segment maps 01 and 02. Boundaries in sections 31, 32, 33, 34, and 35 of T26S R18E, sections 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 of T27S R18E, sections 5 and 6 of T27S R19E, sections 25,32, 35, and 36 of T26S R19E, and sections 13, 21, 22, 24, 25, 26, 27, and 28 of T32S R20E follow natural features (canyon rims) and were drawn by utilizing USGS 1:24,000 hypsography (DLG) and USGS 7.5 minute quadrangles. The maps were overlayed and using the park boundary found on 7.5 minute quadrangles, the best fitting contour line was selected from the USGS hypsography. Lines were drawn to connect the short sections Where the boundary switched from one contour line to another without a smooth transition. T30S R20E sections 13, 14, 15, T30S R21E sections 18, 19, 20, 21, 27, 28, and 34, and T31S R21E sections 3, 4, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, and 24. Boundaries for tracts along the East Entrance Highway listed in deeds 4, 5, and 6 were on-screen digitized using 2009 NAIP imagery and PLSS linework. The right-of-way boundary was created by digitizing the centerline of the East Entrance Highway and offsetting 100 ft to create the easements on either side of the road. Within this right-of-way easement, the tract boudaries were created using COGO commands in AutoDesk using the bearings and distances from deeds 4, 5, and 6. T28S R19E sections 11, 14, 23, 26, 27, and 34. Boundaries for tracks 01-141 and 01-142 found in deeds 10 and 11 were on-screen digitized using 2009 NAIP imagery and PLSS linework. The right-of-way boundary was created by digitizing the centerline of the Highway 313 extension access road and offsetting 50 ft to create the easements on either side of the road. Within this right-of-way easement, the tract boudaries were created using COGO commands in AutoDesk using the bearings and distances from deeds 10 and 11. The Boundary drawn in sections 19, 20, 28 and 29 of T27S R20E follow the east bank of the Colorado River, and were on-screen digitized utilizing 2009 NAIP imagery. The Colorado and Green River boundaries within CANY were on-screen digitized using 2009 NAIP imagery. Seasonal changes to the rivers such as sand bars were eliminated as much as possible in order to best represent the permanent river bank. Boundaries in Sections 35 and 36 of T 26S R 17.5 E and Section 31 of T 26S R 18E follow the county line seperating San Juan county and Grand county Utah. The county line was determined by utlizing a shape file from the Utah State GIS office (Utah Automated Geographic Reference Center (AGRC)). The boundary map was published by AGRC in 2004 and "represents a current county boundary at a 1:24,000 scale. The Utah office of the USDA Soil Conservation Service, renamed the National Resource Conservation Service (NRCS), digitized the data. The source was USGS 7.5-minute quadrangle paper maps." The county boundary was verified by reviewing Utah State Code 17-50-223 which provides a legal description of San Juan County as follows: "The geographic boundaries of San Juan County are described as follows: Beginning on the eastern boundary of the state at latitude 38 degrees and 30 minutes north, thence west to the middle of the main channel of the Green River; thence southwesterly down the middle of the channels of the Green and Colorado Rivers to the southern boundary of the state; thence east to the eastern boundary of the state; thence north to the point of beginning." which is found on beginning on line 1103 of the County Statutes Recodification 2000 General Session accessed from http://www.le.state.ut.us/~2000/bills/hbillamd/HB0130S1.htm. Universal Transverse Mercator, Zone 12, NAD83, US Foot was used as the source coordinate system for the Autodesk Land Desktop project. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Cape Cod National Seashore Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/24/2016 The boundary linework for CACO was generated from the following sources and procedures: Initial GIS data provided by the park GIS staff was utilized. This data had been on screen digitized from georeferenced segment maps and has been adjusted over the years as surveys were conducted and GPS points collected. This data was further refined and adjusted during the digital data conversion process by utilizing high quality GIS parcel data provided by Slade Associates Surveyors for the towns of Wellfleet, Eastham, and Truro. The town parcel data was derived from surveys. The boundary linework that is defined as 1/4 mile from the mean low waterline was derived from the best available NOAA nautical chart, specifically charts, 13249 corrected through April 3/2007, 13250 dated October 13/2001, 13248 dated March 17/2001, and 13246 corrected through December 12/2006. The georeferenced NOAA charts were inserted into Civil3D and the mean low water line was on-screen digitized. This line was then offset 1320 feet (1/4 mile) to generate the boundary line. The southernmost portion of the boundary was taken from GIS data provided by the park GIS staff. UTM NAD83, Zone 19, US Foot was used as the source coordinate system for the Autodesk Civil3D project. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk Civil3D to an ESRI shape file format in a single step. UPDATE: 09/19/2024 Updated geometry and Tract ID attributes to correct errors and account for change orders CACO-CO-FY2024-01, CACO-CO-FY2024-02. Except where noted, geometry was not adjusted from the previous version of CACO tracts. Where tracts were added to fill gaps, adjoining tracts were used to create the new tracts. Adjusted tract ID for 050001A (formerly 050001) to account for disposal. Added tract 194200 using COGO from survey "Plan of Land in Wellfleet, MA #2950 Old King's Highway Prepared for Testamentary Trust Under the Will of Anna Walling Hamburger," dated April 22, 2024 to represent a conservation easement placed on a portion of tract 194168, which had it's acreage reduced. Added tract ID 195081 to represent Round Pond (tract formerly had no tract ID). Added 254095A, an access right of way, to account for a gap in the tracts. Added 255119, adjacent to 195119, to separate the acquired property along town lines (this portion of the property formerly had no tract ID). Added 328714 to represent Nauset Lighthouse Beach Road planned disposal, and adjusted geometry of adjacent tracts 326130, 328710, 326289, 326286, 326287, 316175, 316174, 316176 to align. New tract was drawn using COGO from survey "Plan of Land, Nauset Light Beach Road, North Eastham, MA" dated June 26, 2024 (see bk 1288, p 410). Adjusted geometry of 194169 to match description in deed (bk 1348 p 1103); when calls were not available in deed for COGO, aligned to 2024 Massachusetts state parcel lines. While making geometry adjustments for the easement tract 194200 and planned disposal 328714, cartographers discovered several errors in the Tract ID field and in geometry for nearby tracts. CO-FY2024-01, CO-FY2024-02.

description.gco:CharacterString: Cape Krusenstern National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/31/2022 In October 1994, the CAKR hand-drawn mylar Land Resources Division segment sheets were created. They were continually revised as needed until 2002. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Cape Krusenstern National Monument segment maps by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. using ESRI software in the form of coverages, and, under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. Other digital sources used in the initial digital data set included: best available hydrography and digital public lands survey system maps. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside of the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS and using ESRI software in the form of coverages, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tracts. Attribute and linework errors were resolved, better digital sources were used (DOQQs, survey data, revised USGS hydrography, PLSS, etc.), and land status changes were updated. From 2002 to 2009, many boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the Alaska Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, cogoing the U.S., M.S., BLM, and NPS surveys using survey and Autodesk software, using the written legal descriptions for the park boundaries, using private and federal deed descriptions/plats, NOAA-surveyed shorelines, and using better orthophoto/DRG data to digitize shorelines, ridge boundaries, etc. The CAKR marine shoreline was revised in 2007 using accurate NOAA Mean High Water linework created from 2003 NOAA LIDAR and hydrographic survey techniques. During this time, some boundary linework (with Lands review) was also created by AKRO GIS specialist(s). NPS administrative parcels outside of the park were mapped by Lands during 2007-2008. Encompass converted the data into ArcInfo files, attributed it, and submitted the data each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase created under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team. Specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Also in 2009, the selected native corporation lands were substantially reduced because they had overselected the amount of lands they will actually be able to receive under ANCSA regulations. Hence, the village and regional corporations "prioritized" their selections- (Kikitagruk, Inc. dropped their selections for CAKR in 2008-2009). In 2008, the Cobell restrictions on gov't. use of Native Allotment data were lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. In progress 2009, many of the native allotments are being cogoed-in by Lands Cartographers. 2008 BLM-produced digital cogoed native allotments and other U.S. Surveys are also being incorporated into the NPS lands system after comparing to NPS cogo work or other maps. Tract and boundary data is continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Captol Reef National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 12/09/2012 The AutoCAD project was projected to Utah State Plane, South Zone, NAD83, US Feet. A point shapefile was created in ArGIS. Points were populated using northing’s and easting’s from 158/41,013A (http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/care/Miscellaneous_Maps/care15841013-001.pdf). This shapefile was imported into AutoCAD. Lines were drawn using these monument locations and offsets to define the exterior boundary of the park for the following townships: T26S-R5E, T26S-R6E, T27S-R6E, T27S-R7E, T28S-R7E, R29S-R7E. For all boundaries not included in the above mentioned survey (158/41,013A), aliquot part areas were drawn using the PLSS line work produced by the GCDB files. BLM GCDB digital flat files were acquired for CARE from the Utah State Office. DXF files were created from these GCDB files using LX2DXF.EXE and attached to the AutoCAD drawing. Non-aliquot part boundaries and tracts were drawn using legal descriptions and surveys from LandsNet (http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/care/). 2012 BLM survey information was available for the non-aliquot southeastern boundary of CARE in T36S-R9E, T37S-R9E and T37S-R10E. Utah State Road 24 right-of-way was COGO'd from existing state right-of-way survey maps and aligned to GCDB corner calls. The AutoCAD line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from AutoCAD to an ArcGIC shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Catoctin Mountain Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: This update aims to correct our representation of certain parcels exchanged with the State of Maryland in 1983. The 4 deeds for these transactions were recorded in Frederick County deed BK 1214 on 10/5/1983 at PGs 565-69, 570-74, 575-79, and 580-84. The plats in these recorded instruments (at PGs 569, 574, 579, and 584) inform the tract and boundary modifications authorized by the Change Order. The geometry and acreage of Tracts 01-105 and 01-107 have been modified. Tracts 01-105 and 01-107 are portions of the parcels that Maryland conveyed to the USA by DB 1214/PG 565, which remain as FED/FEE residual tracts after the USA’s subsequent conveyance of Tract 01-119 to Maryland by DB 1214/PG 575, as discussed below. The MLC acreage of 01-105 and 01-107 have been modified. The acreage of these 2 FED/FEE residual tracts has been calculated using GIS because the deeded acreage of disposal Tract 01-119 was not apportioned among its several parent tracts. Tract 01-106 was added to represent the abandoned right-of-way known as the Thurmont-Foxville Road (Route 77), which Maryland conveyed to the USA by DB 1214/570. Tract 01-119 has been added to the MLC to represent the 80’-wide, approximately 1,900’-long right-of-way that the USA conveyed to Maryland by DB 1214/PG 575, for Relocated State Route 77. The USA reserved certain rights when 01-119 was conveyed, which are depicted as retained easement tract 01-119A, also added to the MLC. (Note: Although DB 1214/PG 575 describes the conveyance as a “right-of-way” and does not expressly identify the interest conveyed as “fee,” the fact that NPS reserved an easement and other rights in the land has persuaded NCA Lands staff that this was a fee disposal; in addition, the 1986 CATO segment map (841/92,001) identified this tract as a fee disposal). Tract 01-119/01-119A has been positioned so that it generally aligns with Route 77, but the precise location of the road within the granted right-of-way is unclear based on reviewed records and could be determined only through survey. Tract 01-119/119A have been created as tracts within the park boundary. Tract 01-108A was added to represent certain easements that the USA retained in Tract 01-108, which the USA conveyed to Maryland by DB 1214/PG 580. Tracts 01-108/108A have been created as tracts within the park boundary. The following NPS drawings were examined in the preparation of this update: 841/80444C (2013); 841/80444B (2005); 841/92,001 (1986); NCR 6.6.258 (1984); 841/92001 (1984); 841/92001 (1973); 841/9073F (1954). The exterior boundary of Catoctin Mountain Park was created using coordinate geometry. The following survey plats were used: BLM drawing #841/80456, 841/80422, and survey plat of the Braestrup property done in 2/2/2009 by R.F. Gauss & Assoc. A shapefile for Cunningham State park was imported into autocad andused to help in the georeferencing of data. The source coordinate system for this boundary is UTM NAD83 Zone 18N. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit was created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data was then exported from Autodesk to an ESRI shapeﬁle format and reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude by the Lands Fort Collins Oﬃce. Since this data was created, edits have been made to the original shapeﬁle using Autodesk Civil 3D, ArcGIS Map, and ArcGIS Pro using appropriate local coordinate systems. This data is exported from these environments in either a shapeﬁle or geodatabase format using a North American Datum 1983 projection.

description.gco:CharacterString: Cedar Creek Belle Grove National Historical Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 12/16/2024 Added several tracts into GIS dataset. Tracts 02-185, 02-186, 02-187, 02-188, and 02-189 were created through the subdivision of tract 02-127 in 2015 (see C.O. 11). Multiple tracts were split into two separate tracts due to the intersection of county lines. 02-181 (Fed FEE)-Originally part of tract 02-175. Tract was divided along Frederick/Warren County line. 02-190 (Fed FEE)- Originally part of tract 02-163. Tract was divided along Frederick/Warren County line. 02-192 (Fed FEE)- Originally part of tract 02-171. Tract was divided along Frederick/Warren County line. Other tracts additions include: 01-112 (Fed FEE) and 01-113 (Priv FEE)-Included in original mapping of tract 01-143. 01-144 (Priv FEE)-Tract was created from subdivision of 01-130 (Fed FEE) due to private out sale of parcel 02-183 (Pub FEE)- Tract didn’t exist in previous dataset. 02-184 (Fed FEE)- Didn’t exist in previous dataset. 02-191 (Priv EASEM-O)-outside of boundary, omitted from original dataset. 02-193 (Priv FEE-OR)- outside of boundary, omitted from original dataset. 02-194 (Fed FEE)-Recent acquisition, tract originally outside of boundary, but is identified as FEE due to use of section 6(b)(1) of park law, a minor boundary revision was not performed (See activity entry in MLC for tract). UPDATE: 12/16/2024 Each Cedar Creek & Belle Grove map segment provided by the National Park Service was scanned at 300 DPI and geo-referenced to DOQQs using Erdas Imagine. Common control points were used to register each scanned mylar to the DOQQs. The DOQQs met the positional accuracy that the National Park Service requires. The DOQQs were the primary source used to register the scanned mylar imagery throughout the geo-referencing phase. A pre-existing digital park boundary was provided by the National Park Service and was used to create the Tract and Park Boundary Line coverage. After individual data layers were created for each map segment, the attribute tables were created and proper items were added for coding. Individual coverages had a clipped portion of the Cedar Creek & Belle Grove National Historic Park boundary sectioned off. The individual segmented coverages were used as base layers, while non-existing lines were digitized heads- up in ArcGIS using the geo-referenced scanned mylars. Tract polygons and boundary lines were digitized according to the source. The maps were edited for dangling no des and unclosed polygons. The polygons were then built and labeled. After the polygons were attributed, then checked for label errors and inconsistencies, a batch of automated processes and AMLs were run on the data. Attributed polygons were verified and regions were created. Once the regions were created and validated, ArcMap was used to do a heads-up QA/QC. All data layers were plotted to hard copies and a visual QA/QC was done on the hardcopy. Individual park map segments were edgematched and then mapjoined to form a seamless GIS data model. The finished GIS product was exported to an Arc interchange file (.e00), ArcView ESRI Geodatabase Feature Class (.JSON) and an AutoCAD 2005 (.dwg) file. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

Lineage was overlayed onto 2018 DigitalGlobe imagery within Autodest 2017. Attributes were compiled by PAgis using 911 records. The parcel dataset contains polygon features representing the approximate location of tax parcels contained in County Assessor tax rolls. Individual county data was integrated into this statewide publication by the Arkansas Geographic Information Office (AGIO). The Computer Aided Mass Appraisal (CAMA) systems maintained in each county are used to populate the database attributes for each polygon feature. The entity attribute structure conforms to the Arkansas Cadastral Mapping Standard. The digital cadastral data is provided as a publication version that only represents a snapshot of the production data at the time it was received from the county. Published updates may be made to counties throughout the year. These will occur after new data is digitized or updates to existing data are finished. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

For additional information email anthony_b_marshall@nps.gov Originally Published 2/21/2013: The parcel was COGO'd from survey CHPI_345-60001 which can be found here: http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/chpi/Miscellaneous/. The linework was copied over to either the tract or the boundary layer. Complete tract and boundary topology was then created and exported to a shapefile. Further processing and attribution was completed using ArcGIS. Geometry was then checked and repaired.For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native coordinate system of the DWG was South Craolina State Plane, NAD83, US Foot. description.gco:CharacterString: Chickamauga and Chattanooga National Military Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 09/24/2025 Tract records from a master database were matched and compared with tracts in a draft tract feature layer, developed in 2020 and derived from CAD and county parcel data. A list was made of all current tracts requiring geospatial representation, including secondary tracts. This list excluded records of lump sum tracts that have been assigned tract numbers, as well as deleted tracts. Each tract requiring geospatial representation was reviewed and re-mapped using the following general methods. 1) Tract records that included a complete, legible, legal description were mapped using coordinate geometry (COGO) in either GA State Plane West or TN State Plane, NAD83, appropriate to their location. Although some descriptions predate the NAD83 datum and were likely written relevant to NAD27, these descriptions are generally not as precise as more recent descriptions. In almost every instance these tracts required further alignment to features that are currently represented in NAD83. 2) Tract records described in reference to lots or plats were generally mapped by extracting county parcels, when a visual comparison of the plat and the current county parcel data determined that the lots were well represented in the county data. 3) Tract records described in reference to Georgia Land Lot Lines were aligned to the public Georgia Landlots and Milita Districts feature layer. Where tract boundaries deviated from the land lot lines, they were COGO'd, digitized from historic plats or land status maps, and/or aligned to creek banks or rights-of-ways as depicted in county parcel data and verified through orthoimagery, depending on the information available in the tract descriptions. The lot line data is published in NAD 1927 Georgia Statewide Albers (US Feet), and when the tracts aligned to this dataset were transformed to GA State Plane NAD83 they underwent a small shift of less than 3 ft that is visible at scales of 1:1,000 or bigger. 4) Crest Road tracts, except for the reservations, were derived from a 50' buffer of a road centerline that was verified with orthoimagery. Linear tracts are separated with east-west trending lines that were digitized from historic segment maps. The available land descriptions are not sufficient for mapping highly accurate separations along the Crest Road corridor, but the corridor itself represents the federal ownership along the road to within 3-10 meters (as well as any other tract representation in this dataset). 5) Lookout Mountain tract 07-103 is described in a long, lump sum deed (CHCH 295). Geometry was extracted from the 2020 draft dataset, then aligned to all adjoining tracts after they had been mapped or verified. Where there is not an adjoining tract, 07-103 was aligned to COGO'd boundary linework derived from a 1976 BLM CHCH boundary survey, or the Lookout Creek bank as represented in Hamilton County parcel data. Individual parcels described in the deed have not been parsed out or verified since this unit was converted to GIS format from CAD.

To create boundary and tract line work for the park deeds, legal descriptions, and surveys were referenced and used before any other data sources. Legacy data was used to complete areas of the boundary and tracts that didn’t have deeds, legal descriptions, and surveys. UPDATE: 07/02/2018 The process description for the boundary and parcel data collection was as follows: obtain information from reliable sources such as, deeds, surveys, and other resources. Then the park boundary was generated from those sources. Next, the data was processed using ArcGIS and AutoCAD software. Where legacy parcel and boundary data did exist, it was verified for accuracy then the line work was added to the tract and/or boundary layer. In areas where legacy parcel data didn’t exist for the boundaries or tracts NAIP imagery was referenced to complete the missing line work. Missing parcels were identified and then researched to decide which source would most accurately represent these parcels. Topology was then built, and topological errors were fixed. Then topology was exported to complete the tract and boundary mapping process. All data was then input into Autodesk Civil3D 2009, Maryland State Plan NAD83 feet and verified using USGS high resolution imagery. The Autodesk line work was imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology was developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5 revised 2017. The entire unit was created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data was then exported from Autodesk to an ESRI Feature Class format and re-projected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude by the Lands Fort Collins Oﬃce. Since this data was created, edits have been made to the original Feature Class using Autodesk Civil 3D, ArcGIS Map, and ArcGIS Pro using appropriate local coordinate systems. This data is exported from these environments in either a Feature Class or geodatabase format using a North American Datum 1983 projection.

description.gco:CharacterString: Coronado National Memorial Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 09/14/2023 Tract 101-31 was removed from the dataset per Federal Register Notice Vol. 47, No 195 dated October 7, 1982 which transferred to the Coronado National Forest. Original: The eastern boundary of the park was completed using boundary survey 401/41006 found here: http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/CORO/Miscellaneous_Maps/coro40141006-001.pdf. The western portion of the boundary was completed by using Boundary Survey 401/41005 found here: http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/CORO/Miscellaneous_Maps/CORO_401_41005_0001_of_0000.pdf. The southern portion of the boundary was completed using BLM GCDB data. The northern portion of the boundary was completed using USGS dlg line work. Tracts within the park were completed using a mixture of legal descriptions within deeds, as well as BLM GCDB line work. For the USGS DLG Data Horizontal positional accuracy is based upon the use of USGS source quadrangles which are compiled to meet National Map Accuracy Standards (NMAS). NMAS horizontal accuracy requires that at least 90 percent of points tested are within 0.02 inches of the true position. The digital data are estimated to contain a horizontal positional error of less than or equal to 0.003 inches standard error in the two component directions relative to the source quadrangle. Comparison to the graphic source is used as control to assess digital positional accuracy. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native coordinate system for the .DWG file is State Plane Coordinate System, Zone East, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step. NPS does not necessarily have full fee ownership or hold another interest (easement, right of way, etc...) in all parcels contained within this boundary. Equivalently NPS may own or have an interest in parcels outside the legislated boundary of a given unit. description.gco:CharacterString: Crater Lake National Park UPDATE: 06/05/2017 BLM Township, Range and subdivision line work was used for the majority of the boundary, as well as the tracts. This was done by importing GCDB files for each township and range that encompass the park. PLSS line work was then copied to their appropriate layers for the production of the boundary and tract lines. Tract 01-105 was COGO'd out based on Deed 8 found here: http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/crla/Deeds/crla8.pdf. Tract 01-105 was then rotated to coincide with the bearings of the PLSS line work. The tract was rotated around point X = 4503861.43 Y = 417269.65. For tracts 01-106-01-110, tax lot/parcel data was downloaded from the Jackson County Oregon GIS department. The taxlots were for the entire county of Jackson. The parcel data was then clipped to the city of Medford, and then clipped again to encompass the parcels surrounding the tracts located on Queen Anne Street, and North Central Avenue. The resulting line work was then copied to the appropriate layers to complete the boundary and tract information for CRLA. The tax lots shapefile is generated monthly from over 1,600 coverages maintained by the County Assessment Cartographers. Each Assessor Map is maintained as a separate coverage.

GPS ground survey points provided by the park were also referenced in relation to the County line work to help confirm the tract and boundary accuracy. description.gco:CharacterString: Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 05/15/2012 Montgomery and Greene county parcel data was obtained for digital data conversion. The native projection for the parcel data was NAD 83. The tracts and boundary for DAAV were COGO'd from deeds, legal descriptions, and copied over from the Montgomery and Greene County parcel data. They were then copied to their appropriate layer; either the tract layer or boundary layer. The line work was laid over NAIP aerial imagery for the area as well. For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native coordinate system for the drawing was Ohio State Plane, NAD 83, Zone South, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.
