description.gco:CharacterString: De Soto National Memorial Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 08/07/2014 Line work was digitized from the original Mylar Land Status Map of the De Soto National Memorial in 2002, using AutoCAD Land Development Desktop (LDD) by Avineon, Inc., 4825 Mark Center Drive, Suite 700, Alexandria VA 22311-1846. POC: Xiaodong Hong, Manager, Geographic Information Systems, (703) 671-1900. Email: xhong@avineon.com. Digitized line work was then verified by the SER Office personnel from deeds, legal descriptions, and survey data (when available). Map Projection is Florida State Plane, NAD27, US foot . When discrepancies were identified, individual tracts were re-plotted by use of COGO, using AutoCAD LDD. Data was geo-referenced to DOQQ, Florida State Plane, NAD 83. Topology was created for park boundary and individual tracts. Primary validation of cartographic attributes was verified by displaying the lines in both database and the spatial coverage, but no formal tests were performed. Database attributes were linked during the topology creation process. Database attributes were retrieved from the National Park Service, Management Information System, Master Deeds List (MIS/MDL). Clean Topology was developed and attributes were assigned in AutoCad Map using the Drawing Clean-up function at a tolerance level of 0.10 and Object Data links. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Death Valley National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 09/17/2025 The remaining south half of Section 16 Township 27N Range 1E was removed from DEVA 01-101 and added to the northern portion of DEVA 34-109. Patent 4 issued by the State of California was incorrectly depicted as already conveyed as part of DEVA 01-101 in the National Park Service tract dataset. This parcel will now be included in the adjacent geometry of 34-109. UPDATE: 01/22/2020 Removed 11 acres from tract 52-101 and the unit's boundary due to the final interpretation of the Dingle Act. September 26, 2019 Update: Tracts 151-03 (Bowling Alley Addition) and 85-103 (Crater Addition) were added to the park due to the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act, Public Law 116-9. This law also references legislative map 143/128,605A which has an inset depicting a proposed transfer of 11.1 acres to the BLM managed Avawatz Mountains Wilderness. However, there is no mention of any withdrawal from this unit in the language of Public Law 116-9. This data set retains the 11.1 acres as part of tract 52-101 as per previous releases. NPS is currently researching this situation with BLM and will publish a future update if it is deemed necessary. Tract and Boundary lines that follow PLSS lines were derived from BLM GCDB data dated November, 2014 with some section corners minimally adjusted based on Park GIS staff GPS surveys. Park Boundary was provided by DEVA GIS staff and adjusted to match current PLSS linework. Private inholdings owned by Rio Tinto Minerals were cogo'ed from legal descriptions and adjusted based on high accuracy GPS points collected by Rio Tinto and provided to the NPS for mapping efforts. 28-107 and 28-109: cogo'ed from deva143&0002-001.pdf. 28-104: cogo'ed from deva143&0004-001.pdf. 28-131: Cogo'ed from deva_693-001-01.pdf. 42-108: Utilized GPS coordinates provided by park GIS for the claim corner. 28-105 and 28-106 were cogo'ed from deed deva21. 35-105, 35-108, and 35-109 were cogoe'd from mineral surveys 4292, 4281, and 6747. 63-103 was adjusted based on GPS points collected along the southern edge of the parcel from DEVA GIS. 46-104 was cogo'ed from mineral survey devaca6871.pdf. The cogo'ed linework was placed using BLM PLSS linework. The exact placement of this tract is unknown and will need to be confirmed by locating monument markers. 44-108 was cogo'ed from mineral survey devaca3907.pdf. 36-108 was mapped using GPS points for the NE, NW, and SE corners of the tract provided by Rio Tinto Mining Co. 35-106 was mapped using GPS points for the NE and SE corners of the tract provided by Rio Tinto Mining Co. 35-106, 35-105, 35-108, and 35-109 were cogo'ed from mineral surveys and adjusted to GPS points provided by Rio Tinto Mining Co. 27-105 was adjusted to GPS points provided by Rio Tinto Mining Co. 04-107 and 04-108 were adjusted to GPS points provided by DEVA GIS. 05-104 and 05-105 were adjusted to GPS points provided by DEVA GIS. Tract 15-105 was mapped using the CadNSDI PLSS and adjusted to match a GPS point collected by DEVA GIS at the northeast corner of the tract. Tract 15-10 was mapped using the CadNSDI PLSS and adjusted to match a GPS point collected by DEVA GIS at the southeast corner of the tract. Tract 131-03 was adjusted to GPS points collected by Park GIS staff. The entire section 30 was adjusted to the west based on General Land Office benchmark: 100237. NAD83 Universal Transverse Mercator, Zone 11, meter was used as the source coordinate system for the Autodesk Civil3D project. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Denali National Park and Preserve Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/31/2022 In October 1992, the DENA hand-drawn mylar Land Resources Division segment sheets were created. They were continually revised as needed until 2003. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Denali National Park and Preserve segment maps by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. using ESRI software in the form of coverages, and, under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. Other digital sources used in the initial digital data set included: best available hydrography and digital public lands survey system maps. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside of the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS and using ESRI software in the form of coverages, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tracts. Attribute and linework errors were resolved, better digital sources were used (DOQQs, survey data, revised USGS hydrography, PLSS, etc.), and land status changes were updated. From 2002 to 2009, many boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the Alaska Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, cogoing the U.S., M.S., BLM, and NPS surveys using survey and Autodesk software, using the written legal descriptions for the park boundaries, using private and federal deed descriptions/plats, and using better orthophoto/DRG data to digitize shorelines, ridge boundaries, etc. During this time, some boundary linework (with Lands review) was also edited by AKRO GIS specialist(s) (west bank of the Nenana River using DOQQ's in ~2002). Encompass converted the data into ArcInfo files, attributed it, and submitted the data each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). The Park road wilderness boundary and 1917 park boundary were mapped by the Lands Cartographer in 2005 using the ANILCA legal description. State lands inside the park as well as NPS administrative parcels outside of the park were mapped by Lands during 2007-2008. In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase created under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team. Specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Also in 2009, the selected native corporation lands were reduced because they had overselected the amount of lands they will actually be able to receive under ANCSA regulations. Hence, the regional and village corporations "prioritized" their selections- most of these lands will likely go to patent during 2009+. In 2008, the Cobell restrictions on gov't. use of Native Allotment data were lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. In progress 2009, many of the native allotments are being cogoed-in by Lands Cartographers. 2008 BLM-produced digital cogoed native allotments and other U.S. Surveys are also being incorporated into the NPS lands system after comparing to NPS cogo work or other maps. A BLM survey will resurvey an E-W portion of the park boundary in T. 13 S., R. 7-14 W in summer of 2009. The boundary in this area was changed during 2008 to match the proposed location of the resurvey line. A portion of the boundary in T. 18 S., R. 9 W. section 26-27 was revised due to a new BLM Rectangular Survey of this area. Tract and boundary data is continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude and longitude. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Devils Postpile National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 01/04/2013 Autodesk Land Desktop drawing was defined as CA-North American Datum 83, California State Plane, Zone III,US Foot. Opened GCDB DXF files and defined coordinate systems as California State Plane Zone 3, NAD 27, US Foot. Attached LINE layer from this DXF's to the depo.dwg. These PLSS Layers were used to georeference the drawing. It was determined and then verified that Lance Bishop, BLM Chief of Geographic Sciences for the State of California, that the boundary as surveyed in 1934 (NPS Drawing # NM/DP-4936) is incorrect and should be changed to reflect the 1911 Act that established the Park. GCDB line work was used to define DEPO's boundary. In November 2012 a new survey plat was approved by the Chief Cadastral surveyor. This new survey plat and legal description was cogo’ed out in Autodesk and was subsequently adopted as the new park boundary. This new survey can be found here http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/DEPO/Miscellaneous. The new legal description can be found here http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/DEPO/Legal_Descriptions. Also, new 2012 DOQQ NAIP imagery was downloaded and inserted in to the current segment map for further referance. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Devils Tower National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 12/05/2014 The tract and boundary layers are primarily based on the Bureau of Land Management's Geographic Coordinate Data Base (GCDB) coordinate data. Where the Belle Fourche River defines the tract or park boundary, heads up digitizing in an Autodesk environment from USGS topographic maps was used. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. description.gco:CharacterString: Everglades National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 06/24/2019 The native coordinate system of the dataset was Florida State Plan Zone East, Nad 83, US Foot. The original portion of the park was conctracted out and mapped by digitizing segment maps. Various tracts in the contracted dataset were vastly improved through a throrough review of all EVER Change Orders. Northern portions of the park were validated against Collier County and Monroe County parcel data. The expansion of the park was created using County Parcel data. The data was copied from one dataset to another, and given a corresponding tract number. Parcels that needed to be merged into a single tract were merged as well. Information contained in LRD's land ownership databases is updated daily however tract polygons are posted to the NPS Data Store only when there is a change in geometry. To ensure ownership polygons have up to date ownership attribution use of Lands online map services is recommended. TractsNet AGOL (https://nps.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=e32ce01fad374b1bb9a020c40316ce57) is available to all NPS employees. A public version of TractsNet AGOL is also available (https://nps.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=43bc9db4736140e88e661c67460936e6). Please contact the data originator with any suggested corrections and updates. LRD's boundary polygons represent the current legislated boundary of a given NPS unit. NPS does not necessarily have full fee ownership or hold another interest (easement, right of way, etc...) in all parcels contained within this boundary. Equivalently NPS may own or have an interest in parcels outside the legislated boundary of a given unit. In order to obtain complete information about current NPS interests both inside and outside the units legislated boundary, LRD's tracts files should also be downloaded and used in conjunction with LRD's boundary files.

description.gco:CharacterString: Fort Frederica National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 12/15/2023 Data migrated from CAD .dwg to Geodatabase as regional data standard. Tract 01-117 added to dataset due acquisition on 20200207 using survey plat UPDATE: 03/20/2006 The native coordinate system of the drawing is Georgia State Plane Zone West, NAD 83, US Survey Foot. Information contained in LRD's land ownership databases is updated nightly however tract polygons are posted to the NPS Data Store on a monthly basis. Users can ensure parcel polygons have up to date ownership attribution after the publication date by contacting your regional LRD office or downloading the Current_Tract_Ownership_Data file located on the NPS Data Store (http://science.nature.nps.gov/nrdata/) in a dBase format. Please contact the data originator with any suggested corrections and updates. LRD's boundary polygons represent the current legislated boundary of a given NPS unit. NPS does not necessarily have full fee ownership or hold another interest (easement, right of way, etc...) in all parcels contained within this boundary. Equivalently NPS may own or have an interest in parcels outside the legislated boundary of a given unit. In order to obtain complete information about current NPS interests both inside and outside the units legislated boundary, LRD's tracts files should also be downloaded and used in conjunction with LRD's boundary files. Attribute Accuracy Report for the Hydro Data: The accuracy of the attributes of the source Digital Line Graph (DLG) data is estimated to be 98.5 percent. One or more of the following methods were used to test attribute accuracy: manual comparison of the source with hardcopy plots; symbolized display of the DLG on an interactive computer graphic system; selected attributes that could not be visually verified on plots or on screen were interactively queried and verified on screen. In addition, software validated feature types and characteristics against a master set of types and characteristics, checked that combinations of types and characteristics were valid, and that types and characteristics were valid for the delineation of the feature. Feature types, characteristics, and other attributes conform to the Standards for National Hydrography Dataset - High Resolution (USGS, 1999) as of the date they were loaded into the database. All names on the 1:24,000-scale reaches were validated against a current extract from the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS). The entry and identifier for the names match those in GNIS. The association of each name to reaches has been interactively checked, however, operator error could in some cases apply a name to a wrong reach. Logical Consistency Report: Points, nodes, lines, and areas conform to topological rules. Lines intersect only at nodes, and all nodes anchor the ends of lines. Lines do not overshoot or undershoot other lines where they are supposed to meet. There are no duplicate lines. Lines bound areas and lines identify the areas to the left and right of the lines. Gaps and overlaps among areas do not exist. All areas close. Completeness Report: The completeness of the data reflects the published USGS topographic quadrangle usually, supplemented by Digital Orthophoto Quadrangles (DOQs). Features found on the ground may have been eliminated or generalized on the source map because of scale and legibility constraints. In general, streams longer than one mile (approximately 1.6 kilometers) were collected. Most streams that flow from a lake were collected regardless of their length. Only definite channels were collected so not all swamp/marsh features have stream/rivers delineated through them. Lake/ponds 100 feet or greater in the shortest axis were collected. Note, however, that these general rules were applied unevenly among maps during compilation. Transport reaches are defined on nearly all features of type stream/river, canal/ditch, artificial path, and connector. Waterbody reaches are defined on all lake/pond features. Detailed capture conditions are provided for every feature type in the Standards for National Hydrography Dataset - High Resolution (USGS, 1999), available online through http://mapping.usgs.gov/standards/. Horizontal Positional Accuracy Report: Statements of horizontal positional accuracy are based on accuracy statements made for U.S. Geological Survey topographic quadrangle maps. These maps were compiled to meet National Map Accuracy Standards. For horizontal accuracy, this standard is met if at least 90 percent of points tested are within 0.02 inch (at map scale) of the true position. Additional offsets to positions may have been introduced where feature density is high to improve the legibility of map symbols. In addition, the digitizing of maps is estimated to contain a horizontal positional error of less than or equal to 0.003 inch standard error (at map scale) in the two component directions relative to the source maps. Visual comparison between the map graphic (including digital scans of the graphic) and plots or digital displays of points, lines, and areas, is used as control to assess the positional accuracy of digital data. Digital map elements along the adjoining edges of datasets are aligned if they are within a 0.02 inch tolerance (at map scale). Features with like dimensionality (for example, features that all are delineated with lines), with or without like characteristics, that are within the tolerance are aligned by moving the features equally to a common point. Features outside the tolerance are not moved; instead, a feature type of connector is added to join the features. Vertical Positional Accuracy Report: Statements of vertical positional accuracy for elevation of water surfaces are based on accuracy statements made for U.S. Geological Survey topographic quadrangle maps. These maps were compiled to meet National Map Accuracy Standards. For vertical accuracy, this standard is met if at least 90 percent of well-defined points tested are within one-half contour interval of the correct value. Elevations of water surface printed on the published map meet this standard; the contour intervals of the maps vary. These elevations were transcribed into the digital data; the accuracy of this transcription was checked by visual comparison between the data and the map. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. Flight planning was performed in IGIPlan from IGI. A 500m reduced resolution NED DEM file was used to determine ground heights. A targeted flight altitude of approximately 30,000 feet above ground level was used. A minimum forward overlap of 60% and minimum side overlap of 35% were used. No ground elevation in the project area resulted in source pixel dimensions greater than 1.05m or less than 0.5m. Cessna Conquest aircraft were used for acquisition. Multiple Intergraph Digital Mapping Camera (DMC) systems where utilized in the data capture. The DMC is a digital frame camera that produces a central perspective image with a nominal focal length of 120mm projecting an image on a virtual CCD measuring 13,824 by 7,680 pixels. The pixels are 12um by 12 um. Images from four panchromatic cameras modules, each with a 120mm lens projecting an image on a 7,168 by 4,096 CCD, are assembled to create the virtual frame. Images captured simultaneously from four 3,072 by 2,048 pixel multispectral (MS) cameras with 30mm lenses produce red, green, blue and near infrared images. These MS images are matched to the Pan virtual image using the Post Processing Software from Intergraph. All DMC systems used for capture have been calibrated by the manufacturer. The calibration includes measuring the radiometric and geometric properties of each camera. These data are used in the Post Processing Software to eliminate the radiometric and geometric distortion. The raw captured pixel resolution of the panchromatic virtual frame ranges from 0.60m to 1.04m across the project area depending on terrain height. Each pixel is assigned a 12 bit digital number (DN) by the analog to digital conversion performed after each exposure. Each pixel is resampled during orthorectification to an output resolution of 1m at a bit depth of 8 for each image band. Four bands of data were captured for each image; Blue: 400-580 nm, Green: 500-650 nm, Red: 590-675 nm and Near infrared: 675-850 nm. The final product may only include the RGB data. All aerial imagery was collected with associated GPS data. When possible most imagery will also include IMU data collection. GPS/IMU data were captured with either an Applanix POS 510 system or IGI AEROControl. The GPS data was utilized to control the aerial triangulation process. All imagery was processed through an aerial triangulation in which the airborne GPS data was constrained to expected limits. Analysis was performed to assure that all image frames fit within a strip and between strips by evaluating the image and airborne GPS residuals. The final adjustments assure a high quality relative adjustment and a high quality absolute adjustment limited to the airborne GPS data accuracy. This process assures the final absolute accuracy of all geopositioned imagery. Both signalized and photo identified ground control were used to QC and control the IMU/GPS based aerial triangulation bundle block solution. For each project area the latest NED was downloaded from the USGS National Map Seamless Server website, http://seamless.usgs.gov/website/seamless/viewer.htm, in late Spring 2010. 30 Meter NED was used in all cases. 30 meter post spacing was preferred over the available 10 meter spacing to minimize image smearing and distortions that are exacerbated by a finer, but not more accurate DEM. A visual inspection of the NED using color cycled classification by elevation and a shaded relief was performed to check for gaps, corruption and gross errors. When available the NED was compared to known higher quality elevation sources to detect flaws. Between 20-60 construction points per frame derived from conjugant image measurements performed during aerial triangulation were projected to the NED. The predicted horizontal error for each point was added as an attribute in the SURDEX enterprise database. An operator reviews ortho seams in areas these predicted errors indicate horizontal error in excess of the contract specifications. Any imagery errors introduced by source NED required patching from an alternate DEM or frame of photography with a different perspective. Hardware used included the DMC, various brands of L1/L2 Survey grade GPS receivers, various brands and models of computers, RAID5 storage, solid state storage, NEC brand calibrated monitors, various brands of monitor calibration colorimeters. Software included Intergraph Post Processing Software (PPS) to handle camera raw images processed to virtual frame panchromatic images and four band multispectral images. SURDEX software was used to color correct and remove bidirectional reflectance, vignetting and other illumination trends. USDA APFO Image Metrics are measured and images corrected to conform to the Image Metrics using SURDEX software. SURDEX software was then used to fuse the high resolution pan with the lower resolution multispectral image. This image was upsampled to match the pan resolution using bilinear interpolation and converted to a high resolution image via the Brovey Transform. GPS/IMU data was reduced to projected coordinates in the appropriate UTM zone using the Applanix or IGI office software. Aerial Triangulation was performed using Intergraph ImageStation Automatic Triangulation (ISAT), ImageStation Digital Mensuration (ISDM) and Photo-T bundle adjustment. SURDEX software was used to determine the weak points in the AT construction point distribution. SURDEX software was used to orthorectify the images. SURDEX software was used to compare overlapping orthoimages and correct for minor radiometric variation between adjacent images. SURDEX software was used to calculate the optimal seam path, check seam topology and create master tiles. SURDEX ortho software generates occlusion/smear polygons used during seam review to cut in the best view of steep terrain. SURDEX software was used to visually inspect master tiles for seam and image defects. SURDEX software was used to project and cut final DOQQ image files from masters. SURDEX software was used to create CCM metadata. Lizardtech GeoExpress version 7.0.3 was used to create the CCM image file. SURDEX software was used to measure horizontal error in the CCM. SURDEX software was used to perform final formatting, QC and naming of the DOQQ. USGS metadata parser software was used to validate the metadata. Gear DVD burning software was used to create the DVDs. Various versions of Microsoft Windows were used in all phases of production. For Radiometry, SURDEX Grouping Tool was used to display large groups of images, display individual and group histograms, and develop color correction parameters to adjust image DN. Grouping Tool provides real-time updates of the USDA APFO Image Metrics. The image technician adjusts image correction parameters to bring the radiometric characteristics of large groups of raw images within the Image Metrics ranges. Grouping Tool was used again after DOQQ and CCM production to provide a quality assurance check. Individual DOQQ and CCM may not meet the USDA APFO Image Metrics ranges due to land cover. The goal is to have the state as a whole meet the Image Metrics. To validate the accuracy of the block adjustment derived from GPS, IMU, camera parameters and conjugate point measurements photo identifiable ground control points will be surveyed within each State. Nominally 40 points will be utilized. These points will be surveyed by GPS techniques to produce coordinates that are accurate to +/- 0.25 meters RMSE i n X,Y,Z. The GPS surveying techniques utilized will assure that the coordinates are derived in the required project datum and relative to an approved National Reference System like OPUS. A survey report will be generated to document the point locations, their description, the final adjusted values and the derived positional accuracy. The tracts for FOFR were either COGO'd from deeds, surveys, or legal descriptions, or copied from source data such as the hydro data. The line work was then copied to either the tract or boundary layer in order to build topology.The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Fort Laramie National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 02/10/2009 Established a geodatabase defined the projection as Wyoming State Plane East, NAD83, US Survey Feet. Downloaded BLM CadNSDI PLSS geodatabase file for Wyoming from BLM website. The most current revision date is 9/16/2014. Known PLSS corner errors are +/-128 feet along the southern and eastern portions of the park and +/-63 feet along the northern and northwestern portions of the park. Given the large errors, tract and boundary data were input from legal descriptions and then adjusted to 2012 NAIP surface features (roads, fence lines, river boundaries, etc.) This shift results in a difference between the BLM PLSS data and NPS data to around 40 feet along the southern boundary and around 30 feet along the northern boundary. Tracts and boundary were created using COGO commands in ArcGIS 10.5.1 and exported to AutoCAD for final map production. Bearings and distances were acquired from legislation, surveys, deeds and legal descriptions contained in the Lands archive for FOLA (http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/fola/). Parcels were COGO'd from deeds and parcel data was copied over to either the tract or the boundary layer. Complete tract and boundary topology was then created and exported to a shapefile. Further processing and attribution was completed using ArcGIS. Geometry was then checked and repaired. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native coordinate system of the DWG was Maryland State Plane Zone, NAD83, US FOOT. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Fort Smith National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/14/2017 For the USGS DLG Data Horizontal positional accuracy is based upon the use of USGS source quadrangles which are compiled to meet National Map Accuracy Standards (NMAS). NMAS horizontal accuracy requires that at least 90 percent of points tested are within 0.02 inches of the true position. The digital data are estimated to contain a horizontal positional error of less than or equal to 0.003 inches standard error in the two component directions relative to the source quadrangle. Comparison to the graphic source is used as control to assess digital positional accuracy. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources . The south boundary of tract 01-116 was transformed around monument A-11 ( X = 1275323.85, Y = 392153.57) and A-15 (X = 1275033.26, Y = 392119.17) to account for ground to grid translation. Tract 01-116 was transformed around monument A-8 ( X = 1275303.73, Y = 392745.92) and A-15 (X = 1275033.26, Y = 392119.17) to account for ground to grid translation. The south boundary of tract 01-114 was transformed around monument A-22 ( X = 1275464.16, Y = 392887.46) and A-26 (X = 1275400.49, Y = 392704.95) to account for ground to grid translation. The entirety of segment 02 was digitized from previous segment maps per the request of regional Chief Realty Specialist. The native coordinate system for the DWG is UTM Coordinate System, Zone 15, NAD83. The remainder of the tracts were either COGO'd from deeds and legal descriptions, or Sebastian County Assessor Parcel Data was used in completing the park. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. description.gco:CharacterString: Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 07/24/2018 Source Coordinate System was UTM Coordinate System, Zone 13, NAD 83, US Foot. The majority of FOUS tracts were copied to the appropriate layer (either tract or boundary) using BLM GCDB data. This data was laid on top of NAIP imagery for the park. Tracts 01-119, 01-116, 01-117, 01-112, 01-111, 01-110, 01-108, 01-101, 01-107, 01-136, 01-137, 01-130, 01-131, 01-133 were COGO'd from either legal descriptions or deeds. Tracts 01-104 and 01-132 were digitized from the segment map. Tracts 01-103, 01-124, 01-126, 01-131, 01-132, & 02-133 were divided at the Missouri River high water line to create "A" tracts for each parcel. This was done because of a 2013 North Dakota Supreme Court Ruling, Reep v. State, 2013 ND 253, 841 N.W.2d 664. Missouri River high water line shapefiles were obtained from the State of North Dakota, Land Department (https://land.nd.gov/minerals/mineralapps/OHWM1/Home.aspx) and used as the split line. For transportation DLGs a 95% confidence level is assumed by scale used for adjustments and digitizing, which was around 1:2,000-1:5,000 on average. Accuracy of attribute data is within 90-95% confidence level. The factor which could allow for incorrect attributes would be the length of the ND_Railroad_Centerline arc as opposed to the lengths of the attribute origin arc. Attribute Transfer Mapping was employed as the method of acquiring attributes from ND HUB and NTAD, and the remaining fields were populated based on analysis. Detail was added to railroad sidings and railyards. Railroad interesections were also refined to better align with the imagery. This process provided greater spatial accuracy to all data. For NHD hydro Digital Line Graphs were digitized from the USGS source quadrangle, by either the National Mapping Division, one of their cooperators, or one of their contractors. The digital data were produced by one of the following methods: - scanning a stable-based copy of the graphic materials. The scanning process captured the digital data at a scanning resolution of at least 0.001 inches; the resulting raster data were vectorized and then attributed on an interactive editing station. - scanning the paper map. The scanning process captured the digital data at a scanning resolution of at least 0.001 inches; the resulting raster data were vectorized and then attributed on an interactive editing station. - scanning a stable-based copy of the graphic materials. The resulting raster data were then manually digitized and attributed on an interactive editing station. The resolution of the digital data is at least 0.001 inches. - scanning the paper map. The resulting raster data were then manually digitized and attributed on an interactive editing station. The resolution of the digital data is at least 0.001 inches. - manually digitizing from a stable-based copy of the graphic material using a digitizing table to capture the digital data at a resolution of at least 0.001 inches; attribution was performed either as the data were digitized, or on an interactive edit station after the digitizing was completed. - manually digitizing from the paper map using a digitizing table to capture the digital data at a resolution of at least 0.001 inches; attribution was performed either as the data were digitized, or on an interactive edit station after the digitizing was completed. The determination of the DLG production method was based on various criteria, including feature density, feature symbology, and availability of production systems. Four control points corresponding to the four corners of the quadrangle were used for registration during data collection. An eight parameter projective transformation was performed on the coordinates used in the data collection and editing systems to register the digital data to the internal coordinates used in PROSYS, and a four parameter linear transformation was performed from the PROSYS internal coordinates to Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) grid coordinates. The DLG data were checked for position by one or more of the following processes: - comparing plots of the digital data to the graphic source. - comparing the digital data to the digital raster scan. DLG data classification was checked by at least one of the following processes. - comparing plots of the digital data to the graphic source - comparing the digital data to the digital raster scan. For Montana Parcel Data the General Process is as follows: Download GCDB Download DOR CAMA file Process aliquot parts using ISD created software Proof maps Identify missing parcels Send missing parcels to vendor Vendor researchs missing parcels Vendor converts missing parcels qa/qc database checked for consistancy identify unresolved parcels if under 5% all parcels to convert vendor work done DOR researched unresolved parcels DOR or ISD converts remaining unresolved parcels final hardcopy maps data on ftp and website. The NAIP imagery was derived from compressed county mosaic was generated using MrSID Generation Three (MG3) software using the maximum N-level setting and a target compression ratio of 15:1. All photography was acquired using metric mapping cameras and acompanied by the collection of airborne Global Positioning System (GPS) data. Photography was scanned using Leica Geosystems DSW 500/600/700 image scanners at a resolution of approximately 20 micrometers per pixel. All imagery was aerotriangulated in blocks of 200-1,000 photographs using the Z/I Imaging ImageStation Automatic Triangulation (ISAT) software package. Orthorectification was performed with custom software and the USGS National Elevation Dataset was used for the elevation model. Digital orthophotos were radiometrically balanced in groups of 100-500 images using the Inpho OrthoVista product. Custom software automatically generated the MrSID project parameter file to control the insertion of the digital orthophotos in the final mosaic. The ordering scheme of the digital orthophotos is based on a last-in-last-on-top scheme. Accuracy of NAIP is 1 meter ground sample distance (GSD) ortho imagery rectified to a horizontal accuracy of within +/- 5 meters of reference digital ortho quarter quads (DOQQ's) from the National Digital Ortho Program (NDOP). It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. .The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 05/20/2020 Changed tract 000001 to 101-01 and updated attributes according to the MLC. Originally Published 9/26/2011: Data was created by meeting with planners who used planning maps in identifying the area set aside for the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial. Using heads up digitizing methods , cross-referencing on-ground features as depicted in Ortho imagery of Washington D.C leaf-off dated 1999 and leaf-on dated 2005. This imagery was also the source of geo-referencing, that was done in North American Datum 83, Maryland State Plane, US Foot, in Autodesk Civil 3D. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcGIS shape file format in a single step. There is no defined legislative boundary for the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial, only an acreage figure of 8.14 lieing within east potomac park .

description.gco:CharacterString: Frederick Law Olmsted National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/01/2016 Information contained in LRD's land ownership databases is updated nightly however tract polygons are posted to the NPS Data Store on a monthly basis. Users can ensure parcel polygons have up to date ownership attribution after the publication date by contacting your regional LRD office or downloading the Current_Tract_Ownership_Data file located on the NPS Data Store (http://science.nature.nps.gov/nrdata/) in a dBase format. Please contact the data originator with any suggested corrections and updates. LRD's boundary polygons represent the current legislated boundary of a given NPS unit. NPS does not necessarily have full fee ownership or hold another interest (easement, right of way, etc...) in all parcels contained within this boundary. Equivalently NPS may own or have an interest in parcels outside the legislated boundary of a given unit. In order to obtain complete information about current NPS interests both inside and outside the units legislated boundary, LRD's tracts files should also be downloaded and used in conjunction with LRD's boundary files. For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. The linework was generated from Norfolk County Parcel GIS data and then copied to the appropriate layer. The native coordinate system for the project was MA State Plane Coordinate System, Zone Mainland, NAD83, US Foot. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania County Battlefields Memorial National Military Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 06-16-2025 Modified tracts 01-182A, 03-162A, 03-163A, 04-113A, 05-168A, and 05-169A to show the correct PRIV-Fee interest after disposal. UPDATE: 03-19-2025 To create boundary and tract line work for the park Caroline, Fredericksburg, Orange, Spotsylvania, and Stafford Counties parcel data was used. Follwoing county parceldata deeds, legal descriptions, and surveys were referenced and used to complete gaps in the county parcel data. Legacy data was used to complete areas of the boundary and tracts that didn’t have county parcel data, deeds, legal descriptions, and surveys. The process description for the boundary and parcel data collection is as follows: obtain information from reliable sources such as, deeds, surveys, and other resources. Then the park boundary was generated from those sources. Next, the data was processed using ArcGIS and AutoCAD software. Where legacy parcel and boundary data did exist, it was verified for accuracy then the line work was to the tract and/or boundary layer. In areas where legacy parcel data didn’t existed for the boundaries or tracts NAIP imagery was referenced to complete the missing line work. Missing parcels were identified and then researched to decide which source would most accurately represent these parcels. Topology was then built and topological errors were fixed. The topology was then exported to complete the tract and boundary mapping process.North American Datum 83,Virginia State Plane, North Zone ,US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/21/2019 In June 1993, the GAAR hand-drawn mylar Land Resources Division segment sheets were created. They were continually revised as needed until Dec. 2002. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve segment maps by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. using ESRI software in the form of coverages, and, under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. Other digital sources used in the initial digital data set included: best available hydrography and digital public lands survey system maps. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside of the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS and using ESRI software in the form of coverages, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tracts. Attribute and linework errors were resolved, better digital sources were used (DOQQs, survey data, revised USGS hydrography, PLSS, etc.), and land status changes were updated. From 2002 to 2009, many boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the Alaska Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, cogoing the U.S., M.S., BLM, and NPS surveys using survey and Autodesk software, using the written legal descriptions for the park boundaries, using private and federal deed descriptions/plats, and using better orthophoto/DRG data to digitize shorelines, ridge boundaries, etc. Encompass converted the data into ArcInfo files, attributed it, and submitted the data each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). NPS administrative parcels outside of the park were mapped by Lands during 2007-2008. In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase created under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team. Specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Also in 2009, the selected native corporation lands were reduced because they had overselected the amount of lands they will actually be able to receive under ANCSA regulations. Hence, the regional and village corporations "prioritized" their selections- most of these lands will likely go to patent during 2009+. In 2008, the Cobell restrictions on gov't. use of Native Allotment data were lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. In progress 2009, many of the native allotments are being cogoed-in by Lands Cartographers. 2008 BLM-produced digital cogoed native allotments and other U.S. Surveys are also being incorporated into the NPS lands system after comparing to NPS cogo work or other maps. As a result of the Anaktuvuk Pass Land Exchange, many tracts were created, deleted, and modified in 2008. The Wilderness boundary in this area was also changed as a result of the Exchange. The BLM will survey the rectangular boundaries associated with the Anaktuvuk Pass Land Exchange (located in the north central portion of the park) during the summer of 2009. Tract and boundary data is continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude and longitude. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Gateway Arch National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 12/20/2024 New Unacquired Public FEE tract 01-121 was created and split form FEE Tract 01-110. FEE Tract 01-110 was acquired in 1941 via City Ordinance # 42050, vacating said tract 01-110 city streets/alleys. Portion of the streets/alleys, now identified as FEE tract 01-121 were not vacated via City Ordinance # 42050. New FEE tract 01-121 was created to display USA having NO Ownership in said streets/alleys. UPDATE: 07/22/2024 Tract 08-106 deleted and combined with 08-107. New FEE-O Tract 08-101-1 is part of 08-101 and is outside the park boundary and was created in anticipation of a future minor boundary revision. UPDATE: 10/28/2010 The park boundary was drawn utilizing cogo commands in Autodesk based on the bearing and distance descriptions found in survey maps JEFF_366_3073A dated February 1, 1960 and JEFF_95008 dated September 12, 1995 (http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/jeff/Miscellaneous_Maps/). Tract 01-112, which is the eastern boundary of segments 1 through 7 (Missouri) was drawn using cogo commands in Autodesk based on bearing and distance discriptions found in deed 13. Internal Fee tracts in segments 1 through 7 were on screen digitized by georeferencing scanned versions of the previous segment maps and inserting them into Autodesk. The private inholding known as the Old Cathedral found in segment 5 was drawn using cogo commands in Autodesk based on bearing and distance descriptions found in survey map JEFF_366_307A. Per survey map JEFF_95008, the western boundary of segment 8 (Illinois) is described as the "ordinary high water line" of the Mississippi River. This line was drawn by on screen digitizing the waterline as seen in 2009 NAIP 1m aerial imagery. NAD83 Illinois State Planes, West Zone, US Foot was used as the source coordinate system for the Autodesk Land Desktop project. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Gateway National Recreation Area Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 06/14/2024 The boundaries of segment 101 were updated. The most notable changes are in the Broad Channel area: an acquisition was completed (01-139) which included new boundary survey information; large areas of privately-owned lots were identified out of a larger tract inventoried as NYC property (new lump sum tract), and a large encroachment mitigation project by park staff included several new boundary surveys. There were also minor adjustments to the shoreline boundaries and the creation of the tracts identified for the North Channel Bridge realignment project (01-133 & 01-134). UPDATE: 12/31/2015 The park boundary and individual tract boundaries were drawn utilizing COGO commands in Autodesk based on the bearing and distance legal descriptions found in deeds and surveys provided here http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/GATE/. Boundary line work for the Jamaica Bay was partially derived from deed gate01 which is provided here http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/GATE/Deeds/. Survey 646-80800 dated 03/01/1974 was also used to generate the boundary line work for Jamaica Bay. The aforementioned survey can be found here http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/GATE/Miscellaneous/ . The Jamaica Bay boundary line work was rotated 28d59’13.5" to convert the line work from the Queen’s borough plane system to New Your Long Island NAD83 State Plane system. Tracts 01-101, 01-106, 01-107, 01-108, 01-110, 01-111, 01-112, 01-113, 01-114, 01-115, 01-116, 01-118, 01-119, 01-121, 01-123, 01-126, 01-131 and portions of tract 01-127 were generated from Survey 646-80,800 dated 03/01/1974. According to deed 3 tract 01-103 is “subject to existing easements for public roads and highways…” Survey 646-80,800 shows an excluded area for an existing road that is included in public tract 01-118. Also, the North Western portion of tract 01-103 was created useing the survey named "Breezey Point Survey" dated October 2014. The Northwestern portion of tract 01-106 was alinged to a survey named "Survey of Plumb Beach Area ot Gateway National Recreation Area" dated June 30, 2015.These surveys can be found here http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/GATE/Miscellaneous/ . Tracts 01-104 and 01-105 were also cogo’ed from deed gate03. Tract 01-109 was generated from deed gate01-109. Tract 01-117 and 01-133 were generated from legacy park data. Tracts 01-102 and 01-128 were generated from a property plat of Rockaway Beach drawing number 1002-67. Tract 01-129 was generated from portions of tract 01-103 and legacy data. Tracts 01-109, 01-132, and 01-138 were cogo’ed from U.S. Coast Guard Property Survey U.S.C.G Air Station Metes and Bounds Survey T-XXXX-AD. Tracts 01-135, 01-136, 01-137 were cogo’ed from Floyd Bennett field proposed land transfer to naval station, New York drawing # 81-002-1. Tracts 02-101 and 02-101 were generated from 1974 NOAA shoreline data which can be found here http://shoreline.noaa.gov/. Tracts 02-103, 02-120, 02-121, 02-122, 02-123, 02, 02-125, 02-126, 02-127 , this areas is also known as Fort Wadsworth, were derived from the Topographical Survey of Fort Wadsworth dated September 1985. Tract 02-126 also had portions derived from dwg # 646-41209A. Tract 02-104 was derived from the eastern boundary of tract 02-105, the southern boundary of Father Capodanno BLV, and the western boundary of tracts 02-111 & 02-103, and 0.25 mile buffer from the 1974 NOAA shoreline data. Tract 02-105 was cogo’ed from a survey of Miller Field dated Jan 1971. Tracts02-107 and 02-116 were cogo’ed from deed gate01 survey 646-41121 was also used for ground control points along Haylan Blvd. Tracts 02-108 and 02-113 were established by creating a 0.25 mile buffer from tracts 02-101 and 02-102. Tract 02-111 was established from 0.25 mile buffer from tract 02-103 and 02-126. Tract 02-112 was generated from gatesm02. Tract 02-113 was established by creating a 0.25 mile buffer off the boundary of tract 02-101. Tract 02-115 was generated from deed gate02. Tract 02-117 was on screen digitized using the western side of New Drop Ln. The northern bordered was on screen digitized using the northern border of New Drop High School property boundary. The Eastern portion was derived from tract 02-105. Tract 03-101 was generated from 1974 NOAA shoreline data downloaded from the NOAA website and heads up digitization using 2011 USDA Ortho Imagery. Tract 03-102 and 03-103 and was generated from heads up digitization from USDA Ortho imagery date 2011. Tract 03-104 was cogo’ed from deed gate07. Tract 03-105 was mainly generated by creating a 0.25 mile buffer from the NOAA shoreline data. However, the southwest portion of tract 03-105 was generated from heads up digitization using gatesm03 . Tract 03-106 was cogo’ed from deed gate12. Tract 03-107 southern boundary was generated by extending the northern edge of tract 03-104 to the western shoreline and the Northern border of the tract was generated by using NOAA shoreline data. Tract 03-108 was partially derived by extending the northern boundary of tract 03-104 to the western shoreline. The eastern boundary of tract 03-108 was generated from tract 03-104 the Western boundary was established by using 1974 NOAA shoreline data. Tract 03-109 and 03-110 was created by heads up digitization using USDA Ortho imagery date 2011. Tracts 03-114 and 03-113 were derived from legacy park data and drawing # 646-41972. Tract 03-115 was cogo’ed from deed gate12. Tracts 01-115 and 01-121 were updated to show that the USCG non-directional beacon is located on tract 01-115 not 01-121. The documentation for this update can be found in deed gate17 located here:http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/GATE/Deeds/. North American Datum 83, New York Long Island State Plane Coordinate system, US Foot was used. description.gco:CharacterString: General Grant National Memorial Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 01/25/2007 The county of New York makes no warranty or representation, express or implied, with respect to the quality, content, accuracy, completeness, currency, freedom from computer virus, or non-infringement of proprietary rights, of any of the design, information, text, graphics, images, pages, interfaces, links, software, or other materials and items contained in this dataset. All such items and materials are provided on an "as is" basis, and you are fully and solely responsible for your use of them and for any results or consequences of your use. They have been compiled from a variety of sources, including sources beyond the control of the county of New York, and are subject to change without notice from the County of New York. For the high resolution imagery, The dataset consists of tiled orthogonal imagery produced from nadir images captured by Pictometry International. Automatic aerial triangulation (AAT) was performed. The triangulated frames were rectified to a LiDAR derived DEM. Mosaicing was performed using an automatic seaming algorithm and manually edited to eliminate seams through elevated features where possible. The Park was mapped by using deeds, surveys, and legal descriptions, as well as parcel data for the county of New York. The legal descriptions used were located on the document archives for tract 01-101 in deed 1 page 7. For the remainder of the tracts, the legal descriptions were located in the MIS/MDL under the legal description tab. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native coordinate system of the drawing was New York State Plane Zone Long Island, NAD83, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: George Rogers Clark National Historic Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 08/19/2010 The Parcel data set was provided to personnel of the Indiana Geological Survey (IGS) by Indiana Department of Homeland Security (IDHS) personnel. The data set provided was in an ESRI shapefile format, and was named "County_Parcels.JSON." This data represents a preliminary (partial) set of data harvested through the ongoing Data Sharing Initiative program by the Indiana Department of Homeland Security (IDHS) from local government sources in June 2009, and subsequently updated on September 30, 2009, December 2, 2009, December 28, 2009, February 2, 2010, March 5, 2010, and April 6, 2010. The park boundary was drawn from a survey performed June 30, 2005 by the Denver Service Center. The survey can be found at: http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/gero/Miscellaneous_Maps/gero_440_41009.pdf. Refer to page 12 and 13 for surveyers notes regarding the accuracy of this survey. Tract 01-101A was drawn from a survey by Banning Engineering dated March 11, 2015. The positional accuracy of this dataset is dependent upon the scales of the maps which this dataset is drawn from. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. The parcel data used was produced by counties in Indiana, then provided to the Indian Department of Homeland Security, and then obtained by the Indian Geological Survey. The parcel data was used in conjunction with 2008 NAIP imagery. The DSC Survey was cogo'd on top of Knox County parcel data that was clipped an area that encompassed the park. The coordinate system used was Indiana State Plane, West Zone, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: George Washington Birthplace National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 09/18/2023 Tract 01-113 was added to the tracts dataset, and the boundary dataset was modified to include the new tract within the legislative boundary. The minor boundary revision notice was published in FR Vol 86, No 219, 11/17/2021. The tract geometry was created using coordinate geometry (COGO) from Deed 8 on file in the document archives (the original deed is also filed at Westmoreland County Virginia, Book 960, Page 1477, dated October 3 2022). UPDATE: 03/28/2016 For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). Parcels were COGO'd from deeds and parcel data was copied over to either the tract or the boundary layer. Complete tract and boundary topology was then created and exported to a ESRI Feature Class. Further processing and attribution was completed using ArcGIS. Geometry was then checked and repaired. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native coordinate system of the DWG was Virginia State Plane Zone North, NAD 83, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Gila Cliff Dwellings National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 01/22/2024 Tract and boundary data for entire monument updated to align with BLM surveys dated April 18, 1885 (original) and September 22, 2000 (protraction diagram). UPDATE: 05/10/2004 Creation: The lx12s14w file in the NM23T0120S0140W GCDB file, downloaded in 2003, was used to create and georeference the dataset. Tract 01-102 was created by the section subdivision procedure of the Rectangular Survey System. The source coordinate system used in Autodesk Land Desktop is North American Datum 83, New Mexico State Plane, West Zone, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Glacier National Park National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 12/1/2022 An exchange of land and grants to a conservation easement and sewer easement occurred between NPS and Glacier Park Inc., conveyed/recorded date 1/2/2019. Glacier Park Inc. owns tract 10-105 and granted the sewer easement, tract 10-113-1 to NPS. NPS exchanged tract 10-125 to Glacier Park Inc., but retained a scenic easement over this property, and is now displayed as tract 10-125A. NPS received tract 10-124 as part of the exchange from Glacier Park Inc. Original: BLM GCDB data was used in order to complete the majority of the boundary and tracts for GLAC. This was done by importing GCDB files for each township and range that encompass the park. Where no GCDB data existed for tracts contained within the boundary, recorded Subdivision Plats, Certificates of Survey (COS) and deeds of record were used as a basis for COGO entry. The River boundaries were created by Richard Menicke, Geographer/GIS Coordinator for Glacier. The North Fork of the Flathead River center line was establishing using 2013 NAIP imagery. The primary source of the Middle Fork of the Flathead River was 2005 NAIP imagery in conjunction with US Forest Service boundary data of the same area. 2013 NAIP imagery was consulted in questionable areas. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from AutoCAD to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.
