Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, modifying native corporations/allotments, cogoing the U.S., M.S., BLM, and NPS surveys using survey and Autodesk software, using the written legal descriptions for the park boundaries, using private and federal deed descriptions/plats, and using better orthophoto/DRG data to digitize shorelines, ridge boundaries, etc. Encompass converted the data into ArcInfo files, attributed it, and submitted the data each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). During 2007-08, Lands cogoed in some of the native allotments from the U.S. Surveys and incorporated them into the NPS lands system. During 2008, the common boundary with the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service's Selawik Refuge was revised and agreed upon by both agencies. During 2008+, BLM-produced digital cogoed native allotments and other U.S. Surveys are also being incorporated into the NPS lands system after comparing to NPS cogo work or other maps. Also in 2008, the Cobell restrictions on use of Native Allotment data were lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase created under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team. Specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Also in 2009, the selected native corporation lands were reduced because they had overselected the amount of lands they will actually be able to receive under ANCSA regulations. Hence, the regional and village corporations "prioritized" their selections- most of these lands will likely go to patent during 2009+. Tract and boundary data are continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude and longitude. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Lake Clark National Park and Preserve Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 03/31/2022 In March 1995, the LACL hand-drawn mylar Land Resources Division segment sheets 01-12 were created by the Alaska Regional Office Lands cartographer. They were continually revised as needed until 2003. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Lake Clark National Park and Preserve segment maps by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. using ESRI software in the form of coverages, and, under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. Other digital sources used in the initial digital data set included: best available hydrography and digital public lands survey system maps. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS and using ESRI software in the form of coverages, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tracts. Attribute and linework errors were resolved, better digital sources were used (DOQQs, survey data, revised USGS hydrography, PLSS, etc.), and land status changes were updated. From 2002 to 2009, many boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the Alaska Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. The Cook Inlet shoreline needs to be remapped when/if better MHW shoreline data becomes available. There is also a sizeable georeferencing mismatch between the DRG's and GPS data- especially noticed in eastern LACL. During 2007-08, Lands cogoed in some of the native allotments from the U.S. Surveys and incorporated them into the NPS lands system. During 2008+, BLM-produced digital cogoed native allotments and other U.S. Surveys are also being incorporated into the NPS lands system after comparing to NPS cogo work or other maps. Also during 2008, the Cobell restrictions on use of Native Allotment data were lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase created under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team. Specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Also in 2009, the selected native corporation lands were reduced because they had overselected the amount of lands they will actually be able to receive under ANCSA regulations. Hence, the regional and village corporations "prioritized" their selections- most of these lands will likely go to patent during 2009+ (some of the prioritized selected lands in LACL were recently IC'd or patented in 2008). Tract and boundary data are continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude and longitude. A state tract was created for Lake Clark; OHW was digitized at a 1:800 scale using IKONOS OrthoImage Mosaic or followed available BLM survey data. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Lake Mead National Recreation Area Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 05/10/2018 Tract 03-110 was updated to reflect the plat map NVMS4146. UPDATE: 10/01/2010 The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step. BLM GCDB data was used in order to complete the majority of the boundary and tracts for LAKE. This was done by importing GCDB files for each township and range that encompass the park. Where no GCDB data existed for Canyon Rim portions of the boundary, USGS SDTS hypsography files were processed in ArcMap and converted to converages, then converted to shapefiles. The same data hypsography data used for GRCA was used for LAKE in order to have coincident boundaries. The boundary along the centerline of the Colorado River was completed the same way by using USGS hydrography data as well as the southern bank of the Colorado River where LAKE and GRCA meet. Where GCDB data did exist that coincided with the boundary, linework was copied from the PLSS layer to the tract or boundary layer. In order to map the interior and exterior tracts, deeds, legal descriptions, Arizona State Land Department, Arizona Land Resources Information System data was used. Some tract boundaries were not as definitive. The process for mapping these tracts is as follows: On-screen digitized a portion of tract 06-101 from previous segment maps, starting at point X = 782207.63 Y = 13103198.59 and ending at point X = 847757.29 Y = 12985590.86. All other tracts within LAKE were completed using BLM GCDB data and referencing BLM MTPs to verify. In particular, the aforementioned portion of tract 06-101, as well as tracts 14-101 and 14-102 where LAKE and the Hualapai Indian Reservation overlap. For tax parcels tracts, Las Vegas NV Assessor’s Office data was used. The ALLTAX coverage is a polygon coverage representing tax district boundaries for all of Clark County. This data set was created in part by control points. The AOGPS coverage contains control points for areas throughout the county. Many Control Points for this coverage were originally derived by the County Surveyor's Office by field survey methods, using Trimble Navigation Systems Global Position System Technology, yielding positional accuracy "resource" to "survey" grade, depending upon the method of survey. This data has been subsequently converted by the Assessor's Parcel Data Systems Division from NAD 83, HARN adjusted Nevada State Plane Grid Coordinates in meters, to "Ground Coordinates" in "State Plane Feet". This data is intended for internal Clark County Assessor's purposes only. No liability is assumed by Clark County for the accuracy of this adjusted data. The Arizona state land ownership portion of the land coverage is updated along with the surface parcels coverage. All changes to the surface parcels are performed by the CAD department. They are then given to the GIS department in a DXF file on a township by township basis. Through a series of AMLs and editing procedures, the changes in the DXF file are incorporated into the surface parcels and land coverages. Changes in federal agencies are done primarily through the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) using a customized AML based application of ArcInfo. BLM incorporates its changes as well as others such as the Forest Service, Bureau of Reclamation, Fish & Wildlife Service, National Park Service, etc. BLM and State of Arizona status is updated approximately every six months, other agencies are updated on an irregular basis. Per Public Law 88-639 The inclusion of Indian Lands within the exterior boundaries of the area shall not be effective until approved by the Hualapai Tribal Council. Nothing in this Act shall deprive the members of the Hualapai Tribe of hunting and fishing privileges presently exercised by them, nor diminish those rights and privileges of that part of the reservation which is included in the Lake Mead Recreation Area. Data is obtained from both the Bureau of Land Management and Bureau of Indian Affairs on a somewhat regular basis and incorporated into the land coverage as necessary. UPDATE 04/17/2014: The Bureau of Land Management recently surveyed the boundary of the Mt. Logan Wilderness, which shares a boundary with part of the Park in parts of T33N and 34N, R8W. The data was provided to GRCA by NPS Chief Cartographer, Chief Cartographer, in the ESRI shapefile format in UTM Zone 12N NAD83. This shapefile polygon boundary was traced to reshape the GRCA boundary polygon, where the boundary is shared. GRCA boundary sections that are defined as the “high-water mark” of the Colorado River were delineated by digitizing from two primary data sources: 1) High-resolution (18-cm) color-infrared imagery from the USGS GCMRC (Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center; 2002, 2005 and 2009), and 2) modeled flow lines from the US Bureau of Reclamation (BOR, Wright, et al., 2004), based on 1-meter LIDAR. Both primary sources were supplemented by an ISTAR 2002 Digital Surface Model (DSM), alternate high-resolution imagery, USGS GCMRC modeled flow lines (Magirl, et al., 2008), and on-the-ground mapping. Where using high-resolution imagery, the high-water mark is clearly visible thorough changes in vegetation, soil, bedrock bleaching, etc. This method was used in the Lee’s Ferry area (GCMRC River Mile 0-1.1, river right), near Parashant Canyon (RM 198.2-201.4, river left), and downstream of Diamond Creek to Lake Mead (RM 226.2-273.9, river left). The BOR flow lines were primarily used upstream from Navajo Bridge (RM 0-4.54, river left; RM 1.1-4.56, river right), between Tuckup and Parashant Canyons (RM 165.2-198.2, river left), and fom below Tuckup Canyon (RM 201.4) to below Diamond Creek Rapids (RM 226.2). UPDATE 02/03/2014: The GRCA and LAKE boundaries have been adjusted to coincide with the Mount Logan Wilderness area survey that was conducted. The areas affected for GRCA are T33N-R8W sections 5,8,17 and T34N-R8W sections29,32. The areas affected for LAKE are T33N-R8W sections 17, 18 and T33N-R8W section 13.

description.gco:CharacterString: Lassen Volcanic National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 08/19/2015 Notification of Boundary Revision, published in the Federal Register on July 31, 2015 [NPS-PWR-LAVO-18130; PS.SPWLA0017.00.1]. Notice is hereby given that, pursuant to 54 U.S.C. 100506(c), the boundary of Lassen Volcanic National Park is modified to include 136.69 acres of land identified as Tracts 01-175 and 01-176, Tehama County tax parcel numbers 013-290-01-1, 013-290-04-1, and 013-280-25-1. The land is located in Mineral, California, immediately adjacent to the Lassen Volcanic National Park headquarters site. Also the boundary of the park headquarter (Tract 01-149) was re-coged based on the Record of Survey Map #111/106,260, entitled “SURVEY FOR THE HEADQUARTERS LASSEN VOLCANIC NATIONAL PARK FOR THE US. DEPARTMENT OF INTERIOR, NATIONAL PARK SERVICE SITUATED IN PORTIONS OF SEC, 25 AND SEC. 26, T29N, R3E, M.D.M. IN THE UNINCORPORATED TERRITORY OF TEHAMA COUNTY, CALIFORNIA”, filed in the office the County Recorder of Tehama County, State of California, on August 28, 2012 in Book CC of Maps at Pages 72-74. The survey was projected in NAD 1983, California State Coordinate, Zone 1, EPOCH 2002. A new cad file was created and used to for the cogo-ing the metes and bounds of Tract 01-149 along with the adjacent Tracts 01-175 and 01-176 with an assigned coordinates of NAD 83 California State Planes, Zone 1, US Foot. Later the subject cad file was incorporated into LAVO cad file with the projection coordinates of NAD27 California State Planes, Zone I(401), US Foot.. The Federal Register Notices of Volume 74, No. 206/Tuesday, October 27, 2009, (Minor Boundary Revision of Lassen Volcanic National Park) modifies the park boundary revision to include two adjacent and contiguous tracts. Tracts 01-171 and 01-172 were located outside the park boundary before the publication of this federal register notices. Tract 01-171 is located in Tehama County and Tract 01-172 is located in Plumas County. The legal descriptions both tracts are described as The East 1/2 of the Northeast 1/4 of Section 36, Township 30 North, Range 4 East, M.D.M. according to the official map thereof, excepting therefrom that portion within Tehama County or Plumas County. The westerly, southerly and the easterly layers of both tracts were modified to the NPS layers. GCDB PLSS layers were downloaded from the BLM's GeoCommunicator LSIS system on 20070904 for T39S R6W, T29N R3E-R7E, T30N R3E-R7E, T31N R3E-R7E and T32N R3E-R7E (BLM format). T30N R6E was in USFS format. GCDB was projected from Geographic, NAD83 to State Plane - California I, NAD83, Feet using ESRI's ArcCatalog. These shapefiles were imported into AutoDesk in the PLSS layers. Tract layers were built in AutoDesk using PLSS information (e.g., Sections) as control for tracts. Where tracts followed county boundaries, spatial linework from USGS DLG's was used as reference. Where tracts followed hydrologic features, spatial linework from USGS DLG's was used as reference. Tracts 01-151 to 01-163 are said to have boundaries common with Hat Creek and Badger Flat Road. Good spatial reference was not found for these features so general bearings and distances from deeds were used. Also for the above mentioned tracts that have a boundary in common with badger Flats Road, A ground to grid transformation was applied to bearings and distances entered that follow the road. Corpscon 6.0.1 was used to determine the proper scale factor and convergence parameters to enter. A scale factor of 0.999907691 and a convergence of 0 21 48.99172 was applied. These numbers were derived using 2154542.69497 (x), 440646.449796 (y). The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

Lot 24 (Section 10) was split to create lots 28 and 27. Lots 5 and 10 were split to create lots 26 and 29. PLSS information (i.e., Sections) was used to establish geo-referenced "point-of-beginnings" for these tracts. A ground to grid transformation was applied to all bearings and distances entered. Corpscon 6.0.1 was used to determine the proper scale factor and convergence parameters to enter. A scale factor of 1.000046817 and a convergence of 0 17 32.71394 was applied. These numbers were derived f rom the NE Corner of Section 18, T46N R4E (6683546.35688, 2551772.68101). The resulting tract shapefile was imported into AutoDesk. description.gco:CharacterString: Longfellow National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE: 04/13/2011 Processing of DOQQs included radiometric adjustments made using Earthdata proprietary tools and mosaicking the ADS40 imagery strips. QA/QC was performed to ensure that the mosaic lines were appropriately placed and that there was appropriate imagery coverage. Technicians also looked for anomalies, smears and other indications of problems within the digital orthophoto creation process. Where necessary, tonal balancing was performed over a group of images during the mosaicking process which served to lighten or darken adjacent images for better color tone matching. Two additional radiometric adjustments were applied to the completed orthos in Adobe Photoshop, including a sharpening mask filter, used to help increase sharpness of a digital image. The final digital ortho product delivered to MassGIS was a set of GeoTIFF files in the UTM Zone 19N (in 2008) and NAD83(NSRS2007) Massachusetts Stateplane Mainland meters (in 2009) coordinate systems. Images were non-overlapping tiles covering a 1,500-meter by 1,500-meter block on the ground. As requested by the Mass. Executive Office of Public Safety, MassGIS "deresolved" the imagery in a few areas for security reasons. Using ArcGIS Desktop 9.2, MassGIS then merged the 2008 UTM files into large blocks and projected the data into the Massachusetts State Plane Mainland NAD83 Meters coordinate system. The projection process resulted in a slight offset of large bands of pixels, most noticeable in linear features (like tennis court lines) when viewed at close scales. Tiles were clipped out into new 1,500-meter by 1,500-meter blocks; each image name is based on the first four digits of the X and Y coordinates of the center of the tile in NAD83 Mass. State Plane meters. MassGIS' quality assurance included extensive visual examination for errors, anomalies, spatial accuracy and completeness of the imagery. Because the 2009 30cm imagery was delivered in the NAD83(NSRS2007) Massachusetts Stateplane Mainland coordinate system, the mosaic-and-clip methodology used on the 2008 data was not required. However, the NSRS2007 adjustment to the NAD83 coordinate system was not supported by most GIS software, so MassGIS simply "redefined" the spatial reference of each image to the earlier Massachusetts State Plane Mainland NAD83 Meters coordinate system. This final step did not shift the images or result in any loss of horizontal accuracy. The 2009 15cm imagery was delivered to MassGIS in the Mass. State Plane Feet coodinate system at 6-inch pixel resolution. These image tiles were merged into a single file geodatabase raster dataset, projected to Mass. State Plane Meters at 15cm resolution, and clipped out according to the 2008/2009 ortho index. Assessor paper maps are converted to a form useable in a GIS using one of two approaches: 1. Individual maps are scanned, registered to a geographic coordinate system using a base map, and then lines from the maps are converted to digital form, usually by “heads up” digitizing on a computer screen. The base map is typically an orthophoto base map such as the one available from MassGIS, although it may also be a detailed planimetric base map. 2. Deeds for each property are examined, and the property boundaries are re-constructed and pieced together along with those of adjacent properties based on the coordinate geometry of the boundary distances and bearings. This too results in a digital file. This method costs the most, but provides the highest accuracy result, although this level of positional accuracy is not required for tax mapping purposes. This approach also requires that an individual with suitable experience and professional qualifications be involved in the mapping process. Sometimes a combination of the above methods may be required. Even if a digital file already exists, as it most often does, there may still be the need for a process of rectification which corrects geographic and other errors so as to allow the file to conform to the standard. Both compilation from paper maps and rectification or reformatting of digital files are covered by this discussion of digital parcel boundary compilation. Boundary Compilation Standards Digital parcel boundary compilation MUST result in a GIS data file (the “TaxPar” file) containing polygon features representing tax parcels (see definition) as shown in the assessor’s maps or other sources. Compilation at Level II MAY also result in two other files: the first is the “OthLeg” file, containing polygons representing the boundaries of other legal interests (see definition) if such are shown on the assessor’s maps; the second is the “Misc” file for storing miscellaneous polygons often found on assessor maps (e.g., traffic islands and ponds). Taken together, these files must reflect the best professional judgment of the individual developing the digital assessor map about how to compile existing mapping. The parcel data was laid on top of aerial imagery and copied to the appropriate layer to complete the boundary for LONG. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The original projection of the dwg is MA State Plane, Zone Mainland, US FOOT. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Minidoka Internment National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 10/21/2015 The majority of the tracts and boundary for MIIN were derived from surveys and legal descriptions. The remaining few tracts were derived from the BLM GCDB data. The data was laid over 2011 USDA NAIP, and copied to either the tract or boundary layer. Tract and Boundary topology were then created, and exported to a shapefile. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. Flight planning was performed in IGIPlan from IGI. A 500m reduced resolution NED DEM file was used to determine ground heights. A targeted flight altitude of approximately 30,000 feet above ground level was used. A minimum forward overlap of 60% and minimum side overlap of 35% were used. No ground elevation in the project area resulted in source pixel dimensions greater than 1.05m or less than 0.5m. Cessna Conquest aircraft were used for acquisition. Multiple Intergraph Digital Mapping Camera (DMC) systems where utilized in the data capture. The DMC is a digital frame camera that produces a central perspective image with a nominal focal length of 120mm projecting an image on a virtual CCD measuring 13,824 by 7,680 pixels. The pixels are 12um by 12 um. Images from four panchromatic cameras modules, each with a 120mm lens projecting an image on a 7,168 by 4,096 CCD, are assembled to create the virtual frame. Images captured simultaneously from four 3,072 by 2,048 pixel multispectral (MS) cameras with 30mm lenses produce red, green, blue and near infrared images. These MS images are matched to the Pan virtual image using the Post Processing Software from Intergraph. All DMC systems used for capture have been calibrated by the manufacturer. The calibration includes measuring the radiometric and geometric properties of each camera. These data are used in the Post Processing Software to eliminate the radiometric and geometric distortion. The raw captured pixel resolution of the panchromatic virtual frame ranges from 0.60m to 1.04m across the project area depending on terrain height. Each pixel is assigned a 12 bit digital number (DN) by the analog to digital conversion performed after each exposure. Each pixel is resampled during orthorectification to an output resolution of 1m at a bit depth of 8 for each image band. Four bands of data were captured for each image; Blue: 400-580 nm, Green: 500-650 nm, Red: 590-675 nm and Near infrared: 675-850 nm. The final product may only include the RGB data. All aerial imagery was collected with associated GPS data. When possible most imagery will also include IMU data collection. GPS/IMU data were captured with either an Applanix POS 510 system or IGI AEROControl. The GPS data was utilized to control the aerial triangulation process. All imagery was processed through an aerial triangulation in which the airborne GPS data was constrained to expected limits. Analysis was performed to assure that all image frames fit within a strip and between strips by evaluating the image and airborne GPS residuals. The final adjustments assure a high quality relative adjustment and a high quality absolute adjustment limited to the airborne GPS data accuracy. This process assures the final absolute accuracy of all geopositioned imagery. Both signalized and photo identified ground control were used to QC and control the IMU/GPS based aerial triangulation bundle block solution. For each project area the latest NED was downloaded from the USGS National Map Seamless Server website, http://seamless.usgs.gov/website/seamless/viewer.htm, in late Spring 2010. 30 Meter NED was used in all cases. 30 meter post spacing was preferred over the available 10 meter spacing to minimize image smearing and distortions that are exacerbated by a finer, but not more accurate DEM. A visual inspection of the NED using color cycled classification by elevation and a shaded relief was performed to check for gaps, corruption and gross errors. When available the NED was compared to known higher quality elevation sources to detect flaws. Between 20-60 construction points per frame derived from conjugant image measurements performed during aerial triangulation were projected to the NED. The predicted horizontal error for each point was added as an attribute in the SURDEX enterprise database. An operator reviews ortho seams in areas these predicted errors indicate horizontal error in excess of the contract specifications. Any imagery errors introduced by source NED required patching from an alternate DEM or frame of photography with a different perspective. Hardware used included the DMC, various brands of L1/L2 Survey grade GPS receivers, various brands and models of computers, RAID5 storage, solid state storage, NEC brand calibrated monitors, various brands of monitor calibration colorimeters. Software included Intergraph Post Processing Software (PPS) to handle camera raw images processed to virtual frame panchromatic images and four band multispectral images. SURDEX software was used to color correct and remove bidirectional reflectance, vignetting and other illumination trends. USDA APFO Image Metrics are measured and images corrected to conform to the Image Metrics using SURDEX software. SURDEX software was then used to fuse the high resolution pan with the lower resolution multispectral image. This image was upsampled to match the pan resolution using bilinear interpolation and converted to a high resolution image via the Brovey Transform. GPS/IMU data was reduced to projected coordinates in the appropriate UTM zone using the Applanix or IGI office software. Aerial Triangulation was performed using Intergraph ImageStation Automatic Triangulation (ISAT), ImageStation Digital Mensuration (ISDM) and Photo-T bundle adjustment. SURDEX software was used to determine the weak points in the AT construction point distribution. SURDEX software was used to orthorectify the images. SURDEX software was used to compare overlapping orthoimages and correct for minor radiometric variation between adjacent images. SURDEX software was used to calculate the optimal seam path, check seam topology and create master tiles. SURDEX ortho software generates occlusion/smear polygons used during seam review to cut in the best view of steep terrain. SURDEX software was used to visually inspect master tiles for seam and image defects. SURDEX software was used to project and cut final DOQQ image files from masters. SURDEX software was used to create CCM metadata. Lizardtech GeoExpress version 7.0.3 was used to create the CCM image file. SURDEX software was used to measure horizontal error in the CCM. SURDEX software was used to perform final formatting, QC and naming of the DOQQ. USGS metadata parser software was used to validate the metadata. Gear DVD burning software was used to create the DVDs. Various versions of Microsoft Windows were used in all phases of production. For Radiometry, SURDEX Grouping Tool was used to display large groups of images, display individual and group histograms, and develop color correction parameters to adjust image DN. Grouping Tool provides real-time updates of the USDA APFO Image Metrics. The image technician adjusts image correction parameters to bring the radiometric characteristics of large groups of raw images within the Image Metrics ranges. Grouping Tool was used again after DOQQ and CCM production to provide a quality assurance check. Individual DOQQ and CCM may not meet the USDA APFO Image Metrics ranges due to land cover. The goal is to have the state as a whole meet the Image Metrics. To validate the accuracy of the block adjustment derived from GPS, IMU, camera parameters and conjugate point measurements photo identifiable ground control points will be surveyed within each State. Nominally 40 points will be utilized. These points will be surveyed by GPS techniques to produce coordinates that are accurate to +/- 0.25 meters RMSE i n X,Y,Z. The GPS surveying techniques utilized will assure that the coordinates are derived in the required project datum and relative to an approved National Reference System like OPUS. A survey report will be generated to document the point locations, their description, the final adjusted values and the derived positional accuracy. The field surveying techniques may consist of static OPUS observations, static GPS observations, real time differential GPS observations and VRS observations. The control points were measured on multiple photographs, initially solved as check points and the bundle was rerun including all points as control. After the checkpoint run the residual errors were reviewed to determine the quality of the solution with only GPS and IMU based initial exterior orientation. If the block does not fit the control points within specifications the pass and tie points were reviewed for blunders and weak areas. If, after these corrections were made, the block still does not fit the control well the GPS and IMU processing were reviewed. Once the block has proper statistics and fits the control to specifications the final bundle adjustment was made. SURDEX software was used to predict the horizontal error that results from DEM error using AT construction points projected to the NED ground elevation. As AT points are frequently on man-made and other vertical features not included in the DEM these ortho points can only be used to indicate regions of error by the clusters of points that predict excessive horizontal displacement. SURDEX software was used to measure a minimum of 20 points per CCM on both the CCM and alternate product obtained from the USDA Data Gateway to determine if there were regions of the CCM that may need further review to ensure horizontal accuracy specifications are met. If these areas were found the source of the error was corrected and the DOQQ and CCM were recreated. All products are reviewed by independent personnel prior to delivery. The delivery is checked for omissions, commissions, naming, formatting, specification compliance and data integrity. The native coordinate system for the drawing was ID State Plane, Zone Central, NAD83, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

An AutoDesk project was created and projected to NAD83 UTM Zone 14, USFoot. The project boundary was digitized from maps produced by Schemmer Associates in 1999. This boundary depicts the working administrative boundary of the River and was derived from original boundary maps (1:24K quads) drafted by park staff. The boundary was prepared from source data making it appropriate for management purposes only and should not be considered a legal representation of the boundary. Schemmer maps were imported into ArcGIS 10.2.2 and georeferenced to PLSS linework. Tracts were drawn from deeds and legal descriptions. The boundary for James River Island (Tracts 06-101, 06-102 & 06-103) was cogoed from National Hydrography data. PLSS for Nebraska was downloaded from the Nebraska DNR and from GeoCommunicator for South Dakota. The booundary for Goat Island (Tract 109-01) was cogoed from a Bureau of Land Managment Survey titled Survey of Tract 37, dated March 6, 2009, which can be found on ghe BLM site here .https://glorecords.blm.gov/results/default.aspx?searchCriteria=type=survey|st=NE|cty=027|twp_nr=32|twp_dir=N|rng_nr=3|rng_dir=E#resultsTabIndex=0. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step. description.gco:CharacterString: Monocacy National Battlefield Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 09/24/2019 Secondary tracts were removed from the dataset so that only primary tracts are depicted. 2017:Tract 101-50 was added, in accordance with Change Order 38, based on survey 2004 P.B 761 pg 195 Frederick County, in accordance with Change Order 38. 2014: Tract 101-49 was added based on a survey by B&R design group and Book 1328pg698 Frederick County, MD. 2007: Tract 101-46 was added in accordance with Change Order 36. The new tract was cogo'd by deed in the original dwg file and incorporated into the park dataset. This tract is part of tract 101-41, that was 46.00 ac and has been changed to 25.75 ac to incorporate 101-46. Data was attributed, approved and updated. Topology was developed for tracts 101-41 and 101-46. The tract data was converted to closed polylines and the entire tract layer was exported from the Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format being reprojected to the North American Datum 1983 generic Latitude & Longitude. There is no change to the boundary layer. Deed for tract 101-46 was recorded in book 2114, page 0656 Frederick County, Maryland. Original Publication: This data was originally created in the Autodesk Land Desktop environment via a heads up digitizion of the NPS segment map of the unit. Survey information provided by BLM was imported and saved on the "survey" layer in the mono_seg.dwg file in the NCR Lands Office and incorporated into the final dataset. This data was initially georeferenced using the North American Datum 1983 - Maryland State Planes, US Foot projection grid. The entire data set was georeferenced using USGS DOQQ data. The Autodesk line work was created, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology was developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit was created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map were created. The tract and boundary data was then exported from Autodesk to an ESRI shape file format and reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude by Lands Fort Collins Office. Since this data was created, edits have been made to the original shapefile using Autodesk Civil 3D, ArcGIS Map, and ArcGIS Pro using appropriate local coordinate systems. This data is exported from these environments in either a shapefile or geodatabase format using a North American Datum 1983 projection. UPDATE 04/29/2020 The interest of Tract 101-22 was modified per Change Order 41. UPDATE 09/25/2020 The interest of Tract 101-22 was modified from ROW to FEE, per Change Order 42. This action reversed the change previously approved by Change Order 41. UPDATE 12/15/2023 Tract 01-049 geometry changed because of the survey done by B & R Design Group, job # 14-617. The survey is referenced in Deed Book 10781, Page 0066 in Frederick County, Maryland. Tract 101-12 geometry changed at boundary line with 101-49 due to survey of tract 101-49 done by B & R Design Group, job # 14-617.

No. 1148 (46d53ཚ",121d42ཚ") (Y = 519225.8020, X = 1671037.9896) using the follwoing parameters calculated from Corpscon 6: CONVERGENCE = -0d52ལ.82171" SCALE FACTOR = .999928900 The spatial location of NPS Tracts 01-115 and 01-116 was approximated using Exhibit "A" in Deed 23. description.gco:CharacterString: Natchez Trace Parkway Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 04/12/2016 ROW/Boundary surveys were cogo'ed using bearing and distance calls by UNICOR. Segment maps were georeferenced to the cogo'ed boundary linework and tract lines were on-screen digitized from the georeferenced segment maps. This linework was then sent back to WASO LRD for project completion. The boundary linework was verified by QA/QC of each of the 47 sections of ROW/Boundary survey. Once the cogo'ed linework was verified and correct, each section was rotated to acocunt for ground to grid conversion using Ground control monuments collected by park staff. Once the entire boundary was correctly rotated and each of the 47 sections were matched to align with each other, the tract linework was adjusted accordingly. description.gco:CharacterString: National Park of American Samoa Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 05/25/2016 During the vectorization process of the NOAA shoreline, the satellite imagery was displayed on a computer screen using ESRI's ArcGIS 8.2 software. In order to obtain the highest degree of accuracy from the imagery, the one-meter panchromatic imagery was used as a base layer for digitizing. In an effort to better visualize the land-water interface, the one-meter imagery was overlaid on top of the four-meter multispectral imagery using a 35 % transparency value. The near-infrared band (Band 4) was used in the display of the multispectral imagery. The resultant base layer contained the one-meter resolution of the panchromatic imagery and the colorization of the four-meter imagery. The display was zoomed to the image resolution of the panchromatic imagery and the shoreline was manually digitized. Areas of the shoreline that were obscured by cloud cover were digitized from USGS DRGs. The elevation data are accurate to within the 10 meter contour interval of the original USGS 1:24000 topographic map. The gridded multibeam bathymetry is corrected for platform and tidal parameters and are presumed to be accurate to within a few meters. The derived bathymetry shows a consistant 5 m or greater overestimation of depth in the shallow range (< 5 m) and underestimation of depth the deep range (> 15 m). The National Elevation Dataset (NED) is the primary elevation data product produced and distributed by the USGS. The NED provides the best available public domain raster elevation data of the conterminous United States, Alaska, Hawaii, and territorial islands in a seamless format. The NED is derived from diverse source data, processed to a common coordinate system and unit of vertical measure. All NED data are distributed in geographic coordinates in units of decimal degrees, and in conformance with the North American Datum of 1983 (NAD 83). All elevation values are provided in units of meters, and are referenced to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAVD 88) over the conterminous United States. The vertical reference will vary in other areas. NED data are available nationally at resolutions of 1 arc-second (approx. 30 meters) and 1/3 arc-second (approx. 10 meters), and in limited areas at 1/9 arc-second (approx. 3 meters). At present, the bulk of Alaska is only available at a 2 arc-second (approx. 60 meters) resolution, owing to a paucity of higher resolution source data, though some areas are available at resolutions of 1 and 1/3 arc-second with plans for significant upgrades of the state over the next five years. The NED is updated on a nominal two month cycle to integrate newly available, improved elevation source data. Elevation and coastal line work were followed based on previous boundary maps of NPSA. The line work was then copied to the boundary layer. The road that comprises the southeast portion of the Tutuila Unit was obtained by digitizing from USGS topo maps. UPDATE 5/25/2016: Tract and boundary topology was modified as better road data was available. All linework was prepared to reflect as accurately as possible to boundary portrayed on boundary map npsabm_NP-AS-80000A found here: http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/npsa/Miscellaneous/npsabm_NP-AS-80000A.pdf. Tract and boundary topology were completed for the park, and exported to an ESRI shapefile. There is no guarantee or warranty concerning the accuracy of the data. Users should be aware that temporal changes may have occurred since this data set was collected and that some parts of this data may no longer represent actual surface conditions. Users should not use this data for critical applications without a full awareness of its limitations. Acknowledgement of the originating agencies would be appreciated in products derived from these data. Any user who modifies the data is obligated to describe the types of modifications they perform. User specifically agrees not to misrepresent the data, nor to imply that changes made were approved or endorsed by the U.S. Geological Survey. Please refer to http://www.usgs.gov/privacy.html for the USGS disclaimer. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native coordinate system of the DWG is NAD83(HARN) 02. UTM-2S. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Noatak National Preserve Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 03/21/2019 In August 1993, the NOAT hand-drawn mylar Land Resources Division segment sheets 01-08 were created by the Alaska Regional Office Lands cartographer. They were continually revised as needed until 2003. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Noatak National Preserve segment maps by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. using ESRI software in the form of coverages, and, under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. Other digital sources used in the initial digital data set included: best available hydrography and digital public lands survey system maps. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS and using ESRI software in the form of coverages, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tracts. Attribute and linework errors were resolved, better digital sources were used (DOQQs, survey data, revised USGS hydrography, PLSS, etc.), and land status changes were updated. From 2002 to 2009, many boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the Alaska Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, modifying native corporations/allotments, cogoing the U.S., M.S., BLM, and NPS surveys using survey and Autodesk software, using the written legal descriptions for the park boundaries, using private and federal deed descriptions/plats, and using better orthophoto/DRG data to digitize shorelines, ridge boundaries, etc. Encompass converted the data into ArcInfo files, attributed it, and submitted the data each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). During 2007-08, Lands cogoed in some of the native allotments from the U.S. Surveys and incorporated them into the NPS lands system. During 2008+, BLM-produced digital cogoed native allotments and other U.S. Surveys are also being incorporated into the NPS lands system after comparing to NPS cogo work or other maps. Also during 2008, the Cobell restrictions on use of Native Allotment data were lifted so all Native Allotment data were returned to the GIS/Lands geodatabase. In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase created under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team. Specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Also in 2009, the selected native corporation lands were reduced because they had overselected the amount of lands they will actually be able to receive under ANCSA regulations. Hence, the regional and village corporations "prioritized" their selections- most of these lands will likely go to patent during 2009+ (some of the prioritized selected lands in NOAT were recently IC'd or patented in 2008). Tract and boundary data are continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Ocmulgee National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 09/25/2020 Contact Tony Marshall for update details UPDATE 03/20/2020 All tracts were COGO'd from legal descriptions and deeds. Tract line work was then copied to the their appropriate layer, either the boundary layer or tract layer. Tract 01-110 has no legal description and/or deed. This ROW was verified with the Bibb County Assessors office data and was established by creating a 300 foot buffer around the the transportation data. The NAIP imagery was brought into the DWG for general refernce purposes only. In some cases around tract 01-101, where the boundary coincided with the land lot data, the land lot data was copied over to the boundary layer. For the USGS DLG Data Horizontal positional accuracy is based upon the use of USGS source quadrangles which are compiled to meet National Map Accuracy Standards (NMAS). NMAS horizontal accuracy requires that at least 90 percent of points tested are within 0.02 inches of the true position. The digital data are estimated to contain a horizontal positional error of less than or equal to 0.003 inches standard error in the two component directions relative to the source quadrangle. Comparison to the graphic source is used as control to assess digital positional accuracy. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). For the Land Lot Data, data being transmitted and contained herein represents the best available data as of the date of publication. Every effort has been made to ensure that these data are an accurate depiction of land lots. However, due to the nature of some GIS datasets, some adjustments may have been made to create a state wide seamless data set. The data and information are provided with the understanding that they are not guaranteed to be correct or complete. Users are cautioned to consider carefully the nature of this data and information before using them for decisions that concern personal or public safety or the conduct of business that involves substantial monetary or operational consequences. Conclusions drawn or actions taken on the basis of this data and information are the sole responsibility of the user. This data is accurate for reference purposes and does not constitute a legal survey. rGa & Associates, Inc. cannot be liable for the misuse or misrepresentation of this data. Any errors or omissions called to the attention of the rGa & Associates, Inc. will be corrected and re-submitted for review. By receipt of this data, the user agrees that the data is to be utilized solely by the end users/subscribers making the request of rGa & Associates, Inc. and only for the purpose as described at the time of request. Any reproduction, redistribution or resale of this data is strictly prohibited unless prior consent from rGa & Associates, Inc. has been obtained. For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native projection for the DWG was GA State Plane, Zone West, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Olympic National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 12/17/2024 The draft OLYM tract and boundary dataset on file with the LRD office, which is a reflection of updates recorded from 2011-2019 documented in the previous process step, was projected to NAD83 (2011) Washington State Plane, North Zone, US Foot. The current spatial reference is a change from the 2011 update, which was mapped in NAD83 Washington State Plane, South Zone, US Foot. This change was made to 1) use a spatial reference better suited to the physical location of the unit, and 2) support a planned enterprise environment with better transformation options for datasets referencing NAD83 (2011). For tracts 09-101 through 09-131 and 04-112 all in Lots 12 and 13 of T30N R09W Sec 30 WM also known as the Elmer Day Plat of 1906. I started where the western most lot line intersects the shore of Lake Crescent. I used NHD for the shoreline. The western most line was extended to 980ft (as shown on the plat). This was done for several other lot lines to determine a best-fit north line for the lots. Parallel lot lines were created from the western most lot line at the interval of 100' (or portions thereof) based on the deeds for each lot. The lots were split north and south based on legal descriptions in the deeds for the easements and sales along the corridor for the Spruce Production Railroad to the north. For some tracts the NPS originally purchased the holdings of the railroad company (deed 240) which consisted of a combination of easements and ownership. For some of the tracts (see 9-123), the NPS subsequently purchased the original tract. I am uncertain whether the NPS owns those tracts in fee or just an easement. For tracts 41-131 through 41-147 all in T31N R16W Sec 12 WM, Starting at the east ¼ corner of Sec 7 - BLM point 700540) and used the bearing between this ¼ corner and the center of Sec 7 (Sec 12 not having been surveyed) for the north and south boundaries of all the tracts. Then using the line between this ¼ corner and the NE Sec corner (BLM point 700600) as the eastern line for all the tracts. For the western line, the meander from the previous version (presumably the mean high water line). The tracts were built using the distances from each deed for the north-south dimensions. For tracts in segments 38 and 39, I started with the 2019 version of the tracts and shifted those tracts to better match cogo’ed tracts from select deeds (the entire plat isn’t available only legals from a few deeds), and GPS data for the ¼ section marker common to sections 8 and 9 in T29N R7W W.M., and the IP at the NE corner of Lot 1. The survey 2013_1303004 (Clallam County Assessor V 75 P 005) was also georeferenced as background support. There are discrepancies – deeds in the north ½ of the section used N4°00'33"E as the bearing of the east section line, while deeds in the south ½ of the section used S0°22'23"W. For tracts 12-107 – 12-116 and 12-118 and 12-119 at Barnes Cove, COGO was used for most corners and lines using updated data from 2014 survey for Schweitzer by Johnson Land Surveying Auditor’s File No 2014-1314459. That survey is referenced to the north quarter corner for section 35 (T30N R9W) for which I have gps data. For tracts in the Rocky Pt area of Ozette, 42-153 through 42-167, Starting with tracts cogo’s from deeds (not entirely consistent with 1959 plat by Maris). All the deeds for these tracts begin with the NE corner of Government Lot 5, however a coordinate for that corner has not been determined. A field search for the corner on 8/22/2024 was unsuccessful. Tracts were then translated and rotated the tracts to fit with three gps points for property monuments found along the shoreline. This also moved the nw corner of tract 42-154 to a point relative to the cabin on that tract consistent with the description provided by the tract’s owner. Tracts 19-117, 19-115, 19-116, and 19-118 were cogo’d using the following survey references: Boundary Plan – Headquarters Area Port Angeles, WA. Drawing NP-OLY-8119, dated 1/1962 and City of Pt. Angeles Short Plan JSON 96(03)03 dated 6/23/1997. Tracts were drawn using COGO in ArcGIS Pro. The drawing was aligned and rotated to match section corner points provided by Washington Department of Natural Resources, 11/13/2003. Tracts in segments 21, 22, and 23 (Oil City) were relocated and rotated to align with BLM PLSS corner points provided 10/18/2017. The previous COGO work was not adjusted other than using the Transform tool in ArcGIS Pro to align corners while retaining the existing geometry. The southern boundary of Tract 27-772 was aligned to the northern Hoh Indian Reservation boundary as provided in the 2023 American Indian, Alaska Native, Nand Native Hawaiian Areas dataset published by the U.S. Census Bureau. All tracts in segments 23 and 27 with a boundary adjacent to the Hoh River were aligned to the NOAA Natural Mean High Water line provided 07/07/2011. Headquarters are tracts (19-118, 19-116, 19-117, 19-115) were aligned to the best available PLSS data for the area (WA DNR PLSS corner points), and tract boundaries were COGO’d primarily from deed descriptions. The southern boundary of tr 19-117 and the northeastern boundary of tr 19-115 were COGO’d using plats from adjoining tracts. The following tracts were realigned to PLSS corner points and/or to adjoining tracts that were updated as part of the 2024 boundary review: 19-108 (aligned to WA DNR provided PLSS), 27-109, 27-108, 26-122 (aligned to BLM provided PLSS),Tracts 31-103, 33-101 through 33 -137, and 34-101 through 34-140 were aligned to the best available PLSS data for the area (BLM PLSS corner points) and Tract boundaries were COGO’d from the respective subdivision plats. Tract boundaries adjacent to Lake Quinault were aligned to the USGS National Hydrography Datataset. UPDATE 03/11/2019 The OLYM GIS data was reconciled against Lands MLC database. Tract and boundary topology were rebuilt and any errors were corrected. A complete review of the last 10 years of OLYM change orders was conducted against the unpublished OLYM data. Most of the data was found to be up to date and accurate however the following edits were made. Due to change order 246 tract 21-196 (0.03 acres, Portion of Tax Assessor Parcel Number: 979501903, FEE-O), tract 21-197 (0.14 acres, Tax Assessor Parcel Number: 979502005, FEE-O) and tract 21-198 (0.03 acres, Portion of Tax Assessor Parcel Number: 979501704, FEE-O) were created. The cogo'ed linework was rotated -0d11ཆ.57" around point x=793845.55100, y=900007.92100 to account for ground to grid conversion. Northern boundary of tracts 19-101, 19-102, 19-107, 19-108 in section 3 T29N R6W were cogo'ed from survey map Dawn Lake_1995_0729137.001 dated October 1995. Section 14 T30N R9E. description.gco:CharacterString: Oregon Caves National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 06/14/2021 GCDB PLSS layers were downloaded from the BLM's GeoCommunicator LSIS system on 20070711 for T39S R6W, T39S R7W, T39S R8W, T40S R6W, T40S R7W AND T40S R8W. GCDB was projected from Geographic, NAD83 to State Plane - Oregon South, NAD83, Feet using ESRI's ArcCatalog. These shapefiles were imported into AutoDesk in the PLSS layer. Tract layers were built in ArcMap using the "COGO" Toolbar. PLSS information (i.e., Sections) was used to establish geo-referenced "point-of-beginnings" for tracts. A ground to grid transformation was applied to all bearings and distances entered. Corpscon 6.0.1 was used to determine the proper scale factor and convergence parameters to enter. For Tract 01-101 a scale factor of 1.000058147 and a convergence of -1 58 27.03348 was applied. These numbers were derived from the SW Corner of Section 35, T39S R6W (4138565.37928, 181465.849273). For Tracts 01-102, 01-104 and 01-105 a scale factor of 1.000047513 and a convergence of -2 08 57.31659 was applied. These numbers were derived from the SW Corner of SE1/4NE1/4 of Section 21, T39S R8W (4069656.2738, 196529.444499). Tract 01-101 was redrawn using the 1924 survey information from the BLM's GCDB Flat File for T40S, R6W of the Willamette Meridian, Oregon (discovered by Susan Jordan in the Santa Fe Lands Office). The BLM's LX2DXF DOS executable was used to import the flat file into AutoDesk. The resulting tract shapefile was imported into AutoDesk. 2014 Boundary revision described in P.L. 113-291, Section 3041 was mapped using linework provided by the PWRO Land Resources Division. Boundary linework that follows ridge lines was derived from USGS watershed vector data. Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ESRI shape file format in a single step. UPDATE 06/10/2021 Portion of Preserve boundary geometry was revised based on 2017 BLM Survey for western half of the Preserve in Sections 4,5,8,15,16,17 of T40S R6W. BLM Survey accepted October 6, 2020 and officially filed December 3, 2020.

description.gco:CharacterString: Pinnacles National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 12/15/2024 Revised to include tract 02-104 that was acquired on 01/16/2014. Before the acquisition this tract was depicted like a doughnut hole on the segment map. Tract 03-107 created for possible acquisition. Tract was COGOed based on deed in PTR. COGO closed correctly and POB aligned with common section corner. Checked against aerial photography and aligned with fence line and highway ROW. Adjoiner (03-102) adjusted to align with new tract. UPDATE 07/05/2011 Revised to split the existing tract 02-106 into 02-106 & 02-108 in preparation for the aquisition of the remaining portion of 02-106. Revised on 06/01/2011 to include a minor boundary revision published in the Federal Register on March 3, 2010 that adds tracts 02-105, 02-106 & 02-107. NPS tract and boundary layers were created using a combination of survey information from plats and PLSS line-work from the USFS off BLM’s Geocommunicator site. If the source was a survey, then COGO commands were used to draw the boundary. These tracts were scaled and rotated to account for ground to grid using control. If the source was PLSS, then the line-work was copied. Unfortunatley surveys and PLSS data did not correspond spatially when tracts shared a common boundary. Surveys with good closing errors were given priority over PLSS data. Coordinates for monuments acquired from NPS DSC map 114/41,004 were used as POB’s for certain tracts. However, survey notes are not available and monuments are not always known to be on line. Below are the surveys used (can be acquired from NPS landsnet) in this project and the steps used to draw them. SURVEY-01-125 POB for Legal description of TRACT 01-125 was the NE corner of Section 1, Twp 17S R7E. Bearings and distances taken from plat and entered into Autodesk using the "By Direction" tool under the "Lines/Curves" menu. These bearings and distances were scaled and rotated using the "Transform" tool under the "Map" and then "Tools" menus. Corners POB and the NW corner of lot 1 section 1of Section 11, T. 17 S., R. 7 E. were used as control. Created TRANSFORM-SURVEY-01-125. SURVEY-1924-SIEBECKER POB for 1924 Siebecker survey was PNM corner # 1. Bearings and distances taken from plat and entered into Autodesk using the "By Direction" tool under the "Lines/Curves" menu. These bearings and distances were scaled and rotated using the "Transform" tool under the "Map" and then "Tools" menus. PNM corner 7 (1351572.0900, 417146.0200) and the east 1/16 corner of section 28 T. 16 S., R. 7 E. (1350860.6800, 433090.4500) were used as control. Created TRANSFORM-SURVEY-1924-SIEBECKER. SURVEY-1975-HANNA POB for 1975 Hanna survey was PNM corner # 11. Bearings and distances taken from plat and entered into Autodesk using the "By Direction" tool under the "Lines/Curves" menu. These bearings and distances were scaled and rotated using the "Rubbersheet" tool under the "Map" and then "Tools" menus. The NE corner of Section 1, T. 17 S., R. 7 E. (acquired from TRANSFORM-SURVEY-1989-TAUCHUS) and SE corner of the SE 1/4 of section 12 T. 17 S., R. 7 E. were used as control. Created TRANSFORM-SURVEY-1975-HANNA. SURVEY-1978-HANNA POB for 1978 Hanna survey was the NE corner of section 1, T. 17 S., R 7 E. Bearings and distances taken from plat and entered into Autodesk using the "By Direction" tool under the "Lines/Curves" menu. These bearings and distances were scaled and rotated using the "Transform" tool under the "Map" and then "Tools" menus. Corners POB and the NE corner of Section 33, T. 16 S., R. 8 E. (acquired from TRANSFORM-SURVEY-1989-TAUCHUS) were used as control. Created TRANSFORM-SURVEY-1978-HANNA. SURVEY-1979-HANSEN POB for the 1979 Hansen survey was A-34A (1369719.54, 418124.38). Bearings and distances taken from plat and entered into Autodesk using the "By Direction" tool under the "Lines/Curves" menu. These bearings and distances were scaled and rotated using the "Transform" tool under the "Map" and then "Tools" menus. Corners POB and the SE corner of Section 13, T. 17 S., R. 7 E. were used as control. Created TRANSFORM-SURVEY-1979-HANSEN. SURVEY-1981-SECTIONS13_18 POB for 1981 survey was the west intersection of sections 7 & 8 T. 17 S., R. 8 E.
