description.gco:CharacterString: Point Reyes National Seashore Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 03/24/2026 Adjusted boundary in Tomales Bay to correct numerous topological errors both within PORE tract and boundary layers as well as adjoining boundary with GOGA. Topological errors discovered upon submittal of December 2025 change order (addition of tract 14-189). Change order delayed to provide time to fix errors. Topological fixes will need to be refined with future edits. UPDATE 12/29/2025 Added a new tract (PORE-14-189), approximately 50 feet square, managed by the North Marin County Water District Tract and proposed for donation. Linework in this area needs additional work to properly align tracts and county data parcel data. Likely location appears to be 'notch' in west line of tract 14-119. UPDATE 12/17/2024 Contact Craig Scott for update information UPDATE 10/01/2024 Contact Craig Scott for update information UPDATE 04/09/2015 The accuracy of the data varies depending upon source data used in various areas of the park. The order in which the segments are referenced this metadata are in the order that they were completed. They were completed in a particular order due to a request from the Point Reyes GIS specialist. For segment 01, the majority of the boundary was COGOd using BLM ROS 5 and tied down to the ground with GPS points provided by the GIS specialist from pore. The shoreline was created by using NOAA shoreline data, and consequently the 50 year lease tracts were created by performing a buffer off of the NOAA shoreline. The remainer of the tracts were COGO'd through the use of legal descirptions, and/or deeds. FOPO and SAFR were COGO'd by a previous cartographer, but were repositioned to be tied down to BLM 5 ROS. The "ALCATRAZ LIGHTHOUSE" was roated around point (X = 6006552.64, Y = 2129010.40) to account for the ground to grid translation. Segment 24: Most of the areas on segment 24 were COGO'd by a previous cartographer with the Land Resources Divsion. All notes for transformations are as follows: Survey pore_bnd_t2_3n-r8w was transformed around U.S.C. & G.S. "PACHECO" ( X = 5917751.75, Y = 2229089.44) and AP No. 23 (X = 5928671.75, Y = 2206271.21) to account for the ground to grid translation. Survey pore_641-41943 (AP no. 1 - AP No. 23) was transformed around U.S.C. & G.S. "FRANCIS" (X = 5999043.16, Y = 2122211.80) and Survey pore_641-41945 (AP no. 23- AP No. 194) was transformed around AP No. 30 (X = 5999266.64, Y = 2116745.92) and AP No. 192 (X = 5983656.46, Y = 2087799.29) to account for the ground to grid translation. Surveys pore_641-41941, pore_641-41937 and the east side of pore_641-41938 were transformed around Baker 2 (X = 5986922.81, Y = 2133471.54) and East Peak (X = 5962473.02, Y = 2167452.69) to account for the ground to grid translation. Survey pore_admin_bnd_t1s-r6w was transformed around U.S.C. & G.S. "MOUNT DIABLO 3" (X = 5983946.42, Y = 2127434.76) and "RANGE RESET" (X = 5992071.61, Y = 2132529.94) to account for the ground to grid translation. Survey pore_641-41939 rotated -1d20m43.825s and scaled by 0.999934273 around "Wilkens" ( X = 5927902.29, Y = 2170093.13) to account for the ground to grid translation. Survey 641-41938, only that portion which surrounds Rodeo Beach, was transformed around "ROOT" (X = 5940699.57, Y = 2158773.92) and LEON (X = 5944793.42, Y = 2158966.36) to account for the ground to grid translation. Survey t2s-r6w was transformed around "AP 154" (X = 5980684.59, Y = 2111355.50) and "AP 159" (X = 5980214.80, Y = 2111628.06) to account for the ground to grid translation. Survey t2s-r6w-block-1591 was transformed around "AP 153" (X = 5980994.95, Y = 2111348.41) and "AP 159" (X = 5980214.80, Y = 2111628.06) to account for the ground to grid translation. Tract 02-104 & 02-105 were transformed between station "STUART" (X = 5999979.90, Y = 2141796.45) and "LEDYARD" ( X = 6001283.12, Y = 2140123.71) to account for ground to grid translation. USGS DLG line work for mean high water line of Angel & Alcatraz Islands were used to define boundary. Tract 02-148 & 02-149 were transformed between station "BLUNT" (X = 6007642.05, Y = 2138838.73) and "LEDYARD" ( X = 6001283.12, Y = 2140123.71) to account for ground to grid translation. The remainder of the tracts were COGO'd from either deeds, legal descriptions or records of surveys and were tied down to existing linework. Much of segment 24 and 23 have overlapping tracts between segments. There are tracts along and including Sweeney Ridge that were tied to "FLAT" monument which was GPS'd by pore staff in the field. From the southeast corner of tract 20-111 to the northwest corner of tract 20-108 were cogo'd from BLM ROS, and tied down to Sweeney Ridge survey, and survey monuments. The interior tracts of 23-114, 23-113, 23-112, 23-111, 23-110, 23-109, and 23-108 were created using San Mateo County Parcel data due to lack of deeds, or legal descriptions in the area. Segment 22 was considerably difficult due to lack of monumentation, as well as surveys, deeds, and legal descriptions. This is likely the dataset's weakest area due to lack of data. San Mateo parcel data was used for tract 21-101 to depict the watershed district tract. Tracts 22-101, 22-102, and 22-103 were cogo'd from the BLM records of survey (ROS) 15-LLS-PG028, 13-LLS-PG109, and. 13-LLS-PG108. There is considerable overlap for segment 21 and segment 24. Many of the tracts were COGO'd by a previouscartographer, and his notes are located above. Tracts in the area were tied to existing tracts, except for tract 21-101, which as mentioned before, was created using San Mateo Parcel data due to lack over data for the area. As data becomes available for weak areas, they will be included in subsequent updates. For Segment 20, as mentioned before, Sweeney Ridge was COGO'd from BLM surveys, and tied down to the "FLAT" monument. From the sothern point of tract 20-111 to the northwest point of tract 20-108, a BLM ROS was used to create the boundary which was then tied into the Sweeney Ridge Survey. GPS points from the park were also used to tie the data to the ground at the northwest corner of tract 20-108 as well as the southernmost portion of Sweeney Ridge, as well as the "FLAT" monument. Again, the remainder of tract 21-101 was created by using San Mateo County parcel data due to lack of surveys and legal descriptions in the area. Milagre Ridge was COGO'd through the use of BLM ROS, and was tied to the ground using GPS points provided by the park. GPS points were provided for all the main corners of tracts 20-107, 20-126, and 20-131, as well as the doughnuts within tract 20-107. The tracts were all transformed around point X = 59990877.840, Y = 205954.993. Much of the linework for Segments 02, 03, 07, 08, 04, and 05 were COGO'd through the us of the following BLM surveys : BLM 04, BLM 09, BLM 10, BLM 13, and BLM 14. Tracts on Segments 02, 03, 07, and 08 that were not included in those surveys, deeds, or legal descriptions were COGO'd from the Marin County legal descriptions/surveys that can be downloaded here by searching for a parcel number or map book and map page: http://www.marincounty.org/depts/ar/divisions/assessor/search-assessor-records. Tracts 02-196, 02-101-, 02-192 were on-screen digitized due to the lack of deeds, surveys, legal descriptions and parcel data. Segments 04, 05, and 09-19 are managed by PORE. The tracts within these segments were COGO'd through the us of surveys found from the Marin County assessors website here: http://www.marincounty.org/depts/ar/divisions/assessor/search-assessor-records. These tracts were tied down to known points, and linework such as MUWO boundary, as well as tracts from segments 02, and 03. As new data for Segments 04, 05, and 09-19 becomes available, they will be included in the pore dataset and re-released. Any tract without a deed, legal description, or survey within Segments 09-19 were created through the use of Marin County parcel data. Once the tracts and boundary for pore were drawin, they were copied to either the tract layer or boundary layer. The linework then underwent the topology building process, and was then exported to an ESRI ESRI Geodatabase Feature Class. The Horizonatal Accuracy of the San Francisco Parcel data is as follows: Global Positioning System (GPS) Control Survey: a GPS survey of 65 survey control points was conducted, generating coordinate and elevation data for the survey point network used for Basemap development. The network meets the National Geodetic Survey standard for Second Order, Class 2. Orthophoto accuracy: Ninety percent of points on an orthophoto are plus or minus 2.5 feet of survey point coordinates for the same point. Planimetric features (citylots, sfblocks, cityfeatures, street centerline files) are overlaid on the orthophoto images with an accuracy of plus or minus 2 foot. The horizontal accuracy of the Marin County Parcel data is as follows: Parcel boundaries were digitized from hard copy Assessor map pages into AutoCAD. Georeferencing was based on 400 scale mylar aerial photographs from 1976. Many Assessor map pages did not fit well together. In order to create a seamless layer, problem areas were stretched or compressed. Topology was created in AutoCAD and closed polygons were exported as an ESRI ESRI Geodatabase Feature Class. This ESRI Geodatabase Feature Class was imported into SDE to create the Parcel ESRI Geodatabase Feature Class. No Horizontal position accuracy was given for the San Mateo County parcels. The horizontal accuracy of the NOAA shoreline data is as follows: The shoreline and associated data are a representation based on an office interpretation of imagery and/or fieldwork at the time of survey. The attribute accuracy was tested by creating checkplots of the coded linework. The codes depict shoreline and several alongshore features. A light table review of the checkplots revealed any inaccurate coding. Mistakes were identified and corrected. These attributes were translated into NGS's Coastal Cartographic Object Attribute Source Table (C-COAST) for data consistency. The C-COAST attributes were given symbology and visually inspected to verify attribute accuracy. The horizontal accuracy of the DOQQ imagery should be considered no better than the following: USDA-FSA Aerial Photography Field Office relies on the integrity of the original data collection which was performed by private contractors. Data integrity was validated by the responsible private contractor or sub-contractor. Polygon and chain-node topology present. There are no duplicate arcs and no dangling nodes. The data set contains polygons that do not overlap, there are no polygons that are entered twice, and all areas are completely described. The area features are topologically structured with nodes at all intersections. Attribution of the digital data set includes polygon areas that define the portion of visible imagery used representing the same source acquisition date, with no gaps in coverage. This data set contains imagery from the National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP). The NAIP acquires digital ortho imagery during the agricultural growing seasons in the continental U.S.. A primary goal of the NAIP program is to enable availability of ortho imagery within one year of acquisition. The NAIP provides two main products: 1 meter ground sample distance (GSD) ortho imagery rectified to a horizontal accuracy within +/- 5 meters of reference digital ortho quarter quads (DOQQ's) from the National Digital Ortho Program (NDOP) or from the National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP); 1 meter GSD ortho imagery rectified within +/- 6 meters to true ground. The tiling format of NAIP imagery is based on a 3.75' x 3.75' quarter quadrangle with a 300 meter buffer on all four sides. The NAIP imagery is formatted to the UTM coordinate system using the North American Datum of 1983 (NAD83). The NAIP imagery may contain as much as 10% cloud cover per tile. This file was generated by compressing NAIP imagery that cover the county extent. Two types of compression may be used for NAIP imagery: MrSID and JPEG 2000. Target value for the compression ratio is (15:1). Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. As previously mentioned, pore is in a status of continual update, and as newer/better data becomes available, it will be included in the pore tract and boundary dataset. The native coordinate system for the DWG is California State Plane, Zone III, NAD83, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Rainbow Bridge National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 03/29/2010 The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step. BLM Township, Range and subdivision line work was used for the entirety of the park boundary, as well as the tract. This was done by importing GCDB files for the township and range that encompass the park. The NAIP imagery was derived from compressed county mosaic was generated using MrSID Generation Three (MG3) software using the maximum N-level setting and a target compression ratio of 15:1. All photography was acquired using metric mapping cameras and acompanied by the collection of airborne Global Positioning System (GPS) data. Photography was scanned using Leica Geosystems DSW 500/600/700 image scanners at a resolution of approximately 20 micrometers per pixel. All imagery was aerotriangulated in blocks of 200-1,000 photographs using the Z/I Imaging ImageStation Automatic Triangulation (ISAT) software package. Orthorectification was performed with custom software and the USGS National Elevation Dataset was used for the elevation model. Digital orthophotos were radiometrically balanced in groups of 100-500 images using the Inpho OrthoVista product. Custom software automatically generated the MrSID project parameter file to control the insertion of the digital orthophotos in the final mosaic. The ordering scheme of the digital orthophotos is based on a last-in-last-on-top scheme. Accuracy of NAIP is 1 meter ground sample distance (GSD) ortho imagery rectified to a horizontal accuracy of within +/- 5 meters of reference digital ortho quarter quads (DOQQ's) from the National Digital Ortho Program (NDOP). It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The positional accuracy of this dataset is dependent upon the scales of the maps which this dataset is drawn from. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy

description.gco:CharacterString: Rio Grande Wild and Scenic River Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 03/22/2018 The boundary of the Rio Grande Wild & Scenic River was initially defined per P.L. 95-625 (Nov. 10, 1978) and more specifically described by the approved 2004 GMP/EIS for RIGR in Preferred Alternative B as: "A line located on the United States shores (as set forth in the 2004 GMP/EIS), which includes only such land as is visible from the river and extends from the ordinary high water mark, inland not more than 0.25 mile, whichever is less. It could extend to the farthest sight distance (for example, a canyon rim) for a maximum of 0.25 mile from ordinary high water mark, depending on the specific outstandingly remarkable values present. The segment classified as recreational (Dryden Crossing to the county line between Terrell and Val Verde counties), the wild and scenic river boundary would be 150 feet from the river's edge." An extensive computer analysis was conducted in 2015-2016 using digital elevation model (DEM) data for the river corridor to determine the visibility component, followed by ground-truthing along the entire corridor by NPS staff. The final product is the current digital boundary file used to determine the extents and acreages of the RIGR corridor until land surveys can be completed. This analysis is the most accurate and best available information for determining the current acreages and boundary extents. The final acreages were calculated in grid area (TX SP, South Central Zone, NAD83), with a combined scale factor of 1.00016921 applied to the grid acres to calculate final ground acreage totals. The combined scale factor was determined using an average elevation of 716.42 feet at an average latitude of 29d13'30" N. The southern boundary of RIGR was digitized on-screen at a scale of 1:2400 using 2016 NAIP imagery and is intended to follow the center line of the Rio Grande River. The western portion of RIGR overlaps with Big Bend National Park. All acreages for this section are inventoried as part of Big Bend. Once the tract polygons are created, this layer is exported for use with AutoCAD or reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude for posting to the IRMA portal. Topology rules and are developed for both the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5.

description.gco:CharacterString: River Raisin National Battlefield Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 03/30/2015 The park boundary was COGO'd from Deed 1 found here: http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/RIRA/Deeds/RIRA%20Deed%2010-12-10.pdf. The line work was overlayed with 2009 NAIP imager for the area. Tract 101-02 drawn from a draft survey and legal by Johnson & Anderson. Tract 101-03 was cogo'd from parcel dimensions provided on the City of Monroe GIS web page https://cityofmonroegis.monroemi.gov/Apps/GISViewer/. Tract 102-01 was drawn from a survey dated 2/14/2018 by Johnson & Anderson. Tract 102-02 was drawn from a survey conducted by Michigan Surveying, Inc. dated 8/4/14 and was rotated 9.78 degrees to match up with Tract 102-03. Tract 102-03 was drawn from a survey conducted by Michigan Surveying, Inc. dated 11/01/13 and rotated 4d55པ" around 13436402.40E, 200019.59N to account for ground to grid. 102-04 was drawn from a map on the Brownstown Township Assessor's page here https://is.bsasoftware.com/bsa.is/AssessingServices/ServiceAssessingAttachmentDetail.aspx?p=70+171+99+0014+000&dp=70+171+99+0014+000&i=1&appid=0&actSn=0&actSna=W+JEFFERSON+AVE&uskchid=6516&unit=415&fn=70+171+99+0014+000&caption=No+caption+found&tp=a. Once the tract/boundary was COGO'd, the line work was copied to the appropriate layer. Tract and boundary topology were then built and exported to a shapefile projected to LL83. For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native projection of the DWG was NAD 83 Michigan State Plane, South Zone, US FOOT. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Roger Williams National Memorial Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 10/27/2011 For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The park boundary was cogo'd from deeds and then overlaid on top of NAIP imagery. The linework was then copied over to the boundary layer and topology was built and exported to shapefile. The native projection of the drawing is Rhode Island State Plane zone, NAD 83, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Saint Croix Island International Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 06/13/2016 Tract 01-109 geometry was added to the park to portray the lighthouse reservation. The legal description/survey information used was from Deed 2 found here: http://landsnet.nps.gov/tractsnet/documents/sacr/deeds. UPDATE 04/29/2013 SACR was mapped using a combination of parcel data, legal descriptions, as well as source data such as NOAA RNC's and NAIP imagery. Tracts that have a web boundary used the NOAA RNC data. Land-based tracts either used legal descriptions from the MIS/MDL, legal descriptions from deeds, parcel data, or a combination thereof. The data should be considered no better than the source data used to complete the mapping of SACR. UPDATE 04/28/2013 The NOAA ENC® Direct to GIS data is derived from data that conforms to the International Hydrographic Organization Transfer Standard for Digital Hydrographic Data, Special Publication S-57, ENC Product Specification Edition 2.0. The NOAA ENC® database has been built from a combination of charted information as well as original "source" information. NOAA has compiled critical features such as channel limits, aids to navigation, and obstructions from the original documents that were used to put the feature on the paper chart. The objective is to use the most accurate information for features that are critical to the safety of navigation. NOAA uses a number of sources in compiling NOAA ENC®S including U.S. Army Corps of Engineers surveys, drawings, and permits, U.S. Coast Guard Local Notices to Mariner, National Imagery and Mapping Agency Notices to Mariners, NOAA hydrographic surveys, and the largest scale paper chart of an area. ENC® Direct to GIS data was created by transforming Approach and Harbor NOAA ENC® version 2 cells to ESRI's shapefile format using Safe Software's Feature Manipulation Engine. For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. Flight planning was performed in IGIPlan from IGI. A 500m reduced resolution NED DEM file was used to determine ground heights. A targeted flight altitude of approximately 30,000 feet above ground level was used. A minimum forward overlap of 60% and minimum side overlap of 35% were used. No ground elevation in the project area resulted in source pixel dimensions greater than 1.05m or less than 0.5m. Cessna Conquest aircraft were used for acquisition. Multiple Intergraph Digital Mapping Camera (DMC) systems where utilized in the data capture. The DMC is a digital frame camera that produces a central perspective image with a nominal focal length of 120mm projecting an image on a virtual CCD measuring 13,824 by 7,680 pixels. The pixels are 12um by 12 um. Images from four panchromatic cameras modules, each with a 120mm lens projecting an image on a 7,168 by 4,096 CCD, are assembled to create the virtual frame. Images captured simultaneously from four 3,072 by 2,048 pixel multispectral (MS) cameras with 30mm lenses produce red, green, blue and near infrared images. These MS images are matched to the Pan virtual image using the Post Processing Software from Intergraph. All DMC systems used for capture have been calibrated by the manufacturer. The calibration includes measuring the radiometric and geometric properties of each camera. These data are used in the Post Processing Software to eliminate the radiometric and geometric distortion. The raw captured pixel resolution of the panchromatic virtual frame ranges from 0.60m to 1.04m across the project area depending on terrain height. Each pixel is assigned a 12 bit digital number (DN) by the analog to digital conversion performed after each exposure. Each pixel is resampled during orthorectification to an output resolution of 1m at a bit depth of 8 for each image band. Four bands of data were captured for each image; Blue: 400-580 nm, Green: 500-650 nm, Red: 590-675 nm and Near infrared: 675-850 nm. The final product may only include the RGB data. All aerial imagery was collected with associated GPS data. When possible most imagery will also include IMU data collection. GPS/IMU data were captured with either an Applanix POS 510 system or IGI AEROControl. The GPS data was utilized to control the aerial triangulation process. All imagery was processed through an aerial triangulation in which the airborne GPS data was constrained to expected limits. Analysis was performed to assure that all image frames fit within a strip and between strips by evaluating the image and airborne GPS residuals. The final adjustments assure a high quality relative adjustment and a high quality absolute adjustment limited to the airborne GPS data accuracy. This process assures the final absolute accuracy of all geopositioned imagery. Both signalized and photo identified ground control were used to QC and control the IMU/GPS based aerial triangulation bundle block solution. For each project area the latest NED was downloaded from the USGS National Map Seamless Server website, http://seamless.usgs.gov/website/seamless/viewer.htm, in late Spring 2010. 30 Meter NED was used in all cases. 30 meter post spacing was preferred over the available 10 meter spacing to minimize image smearing and distortions that are exacerbated by a finer, but not more accurate DEM. A visual inspection of the NED using color cycled classification by elevation and a shaded relief was performed to check for gaps, corruption and gross errors. When available the NED was compared to known higher quality elevation sources to detect flaws. Between 20-60 construction points per frame derived from conjugant image measurements performed during aerial triangulation were projected to the NED. The predicted horizontal error for each point was added as an attribute in the SURDEX enterprise database. An operator reviews ortho seams in areas these predicted errors indicate horizontal error in excess of the contract specifications. Any imagery errors introduced by source NED required patching from an alternate DEM or frame of photography with a different perspective. Hardware used included the DMC, various brands of L1/L2 Survey grade GPS receivers, various brands and models of computers, RAID5 storage, solid state storage, NEC brand calibrated monitors, various brands of monitor calibration colorimeters. Software included Intergraph Post Processing Software (PPS) to handle camera raw images processed to virtual frame panchromatic images and four band multispectral images. SURDEX software was used to color correct and remove bidirectional reflectance, vignetting and other illumination trends. USDA APFO Image Metrics are measured and images corrected to conform to the Image Metrics using SURDEX software. SURDEX software was then used to fuse the high resolution pan with the lower resolution multispectral image. This image was upsampled to match the pan resolution using bilinear interpolation and converted to a high resolution image via the Brovey Transform. GPS/IMU data was reduced to projected coordinates in the appropriate UTM zone using the Applanix or IGI office software. Aerial Triangulation was performed using Intergraph ImageStation Automatic Triangulation (ISAT), ImageStation Digital Mensuration (ISDM) and Photo-T bundle adjustment. SURDEX software was used to determine the weak points in the AT construction point distribution. SURDEX software was used to orthorectify the images. SURDEX software was used to compare overlapping orthoimages and correct for minor radiometric variation between adjacent images. SURDEX software was used to calculate the optimal seam path, check seam topology and create master tiles. SURDEX ortho software generates occlusion/smear polygons used during seam review to cut in the best view of steep terrain. SURDEX software was used to visually inspect master tiles for seam and image defects. SURDEX software was used to project and cut final DOQQ image files from masters. SURDEX software was used to create CCM metadata. Lizardtech GeoExpress version 7.0.3 was used to create the CCM image file. SURDEX software was used to measure horizontal error in the CCM. SURDEX software was used to perform final formatting, QC and naming of the DOQQ. USGS metadata parser software was used to validate the metadata. Gear DVD burning software was used to create the DVDs. Various versions of Microsoft Windows were used in all phases of production. For Radiometry, SURDEX Grouping Tool was used to display large groups of images, display individual and group histograms, and develop color correction parameters to adjust image DN. Grouping Tool provides real-time updates of the USDA APFO Image Metrics. The image technician adjusts image correction parameters to bring the radiometric characteristics of large groups of raw images within the Image Metrics ranges. Grouping Tool was used again after DOQQ and CCM production to provide a quality assurance check. Individual DOQQ and CCM may not meet the USDA APFO Image Metrics ranges due to land cover. The goal is to have the state as a whole meet the Image Metrics. To validate the accuracy of the block adjustment derived from GPS, IMU, camera parameters and conjugate point measurements photo identifiable ground control points will be surveyed within each State. Nominally 40 points will be utilized. These points will be surveyed by GPS techniques to produce coordinates that are accurate to +/- 0.25 meters RMSE i n X,Y,Z. The GPS surveying techniques utilized will assure that the coordinates are derived in the required project datum and relative to an approved National Reference System like OPUS. A survey report will be generated to document the point locations, their description, the final adjusted values and the derived positional accuracy. The field surveying techniques may consist of static OPUS observations, static GPS observations, real time differential GPS observations and VRS observations. The control points were measured on multiple photographs, initially solved as check points and the bundle was rerun including all points as control. After the checkpoint run the residual errors were reviewed to determine the quality of the solution with only GPS and IMU based initial exterior orientation. If the block does not fit the control points within specifications the pass and tie points were reviewed for blunders and weak areas. If, after these corrections were made, the block still does not fit the control well the GPS and IMU processing were reviewed. Once the block has proper statistics and fits the control to specifications the final bundle adjustment was made. SURDEX software was used to predict the horizontal error that results from DEM error using AT construction points projected to the NED ground elevation. As AT points are frequently on man-made and other vertical features not included in the DEM these ortho points can only be used to indicate regions of error by the clusters of points that predict excessive horizontal displacement. SURDEX software was used to measure a minimum of 20 points per CCM on both the CCM and alternate product obtained from the USDA Data Gateway to determine if there were regions of the CCM that may need further review to ensure horizontal accuracy specifications are met. If these areas were found the source of the error was corrected and the DOQQ and CCM were recreated. All products are reviewed by independent personnel prior to delivery. The delivery is checked for omissions, commissions, naming, formatting, specification compliance and data integrity. The native coordinate sytem of the DWG is Maine State Plane, Zone East, NAD 83, US Foot. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Salinas Pueblo Missions National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 08/29/2025 Tract 102-12 divided to capture change in ownership of road that was not previously captured in data. State highway 513 extends from the junction of U.S. 60 northerly to the Abo State Monument, being approximately 0.7 miles in length. Torrance County road B005 (tract 102-25) extends northerly from the termination of State Highway 513. UPDATE 06/13/2025 Tract 102-34 created via deed description and survey by Douglas Critchfield (RLS 11222), February 2, 2023. In addition, tract and boundary data for all three units were adjusted to align with BLM PLSS data/surveys. UPDATE 06/01/2011 Information contained in LRD's land ownership databases is updated nightly however tract polygons are posted to the NPS Data Store on a monthly basis. Users can ensure parcel polygons have up to date ownership attribution after the publication date by contacting your regional LRD office or downloading the Current_Tract_Ownership_Data file located on the NPS Data Store (http://science.nature.nps.gov/nrdata/) in a dBase format. Please contact the data originator with any suggested corrections and updates. LRD's boundary polygons represent the current legislated boundary of a given NPS unit. NPS does not necessarily have full fee ownership or hold another interest (easement, right of way, etc...) in all parcels contained within this boundary. Equivalently NPS may own or have an interest in parcels outside the legislated boundary of a given unit. In order to obtain complete information about current NPS interests both inside and outside the units legislated boundary, LRD's tracts files should also be downloaded and used in conjunction with LRD's boundary files. The tracts and boundary were COGO'd from deeds, legal descriptions, and miscellaneous maps. Any remaining tracts or boundary lines were copied from BLM GCDB and moved to their respective layer. Tract 102-12 was copied from USGS Transportation DLGs. Tract 102-25 was on-screen digitized from the previous segment map. Tracts 102-17, 102-09, 102-24, and 102-23 were COGO'd from survey sapu313&0001-001.pdf. For the USGS DLG Data Horizontal positional accuracy is based upon the use of USGS source quadrangles which are compiled to meet National Map Accuracy Standards (NMAS). NMAS horizontal accuracy requires that at least 90 percent of points tested are within 0.02 inches of the true position. The digital data are estimated to contain a horizontal positional error of less than or equal to 0.003 inches standard error in the two component directions relative to the source quadrangle. Comparison to the graphic source is used as control to assess digital positional accuracy. For the BLM GCDB Data the majority of coordinates in this dataset fall within +/- 40 feet spatial accuracy (the general rule of thumb to be called 1:24,000-scale data). For the DOQQs the horizontal positional accuracy and the assurance of that accuracy depend, in part, on the accuracy of the data inputs to the rectification process. These inputs consist of the digital elevation model (DEM),aerotriangulation control and methods, the photo source camera calibration, scanner calibration, and aerial photographs that meet National Aerial Photography Program (NAPP) standards. The vertical accuracy of the verified USGS format DEM is equivalent to or better than a USGS level 1 or 2 DEM, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of no greater than 7.0 meters. Field control is acquired by third order class 1 or better survey methods sufficiently spaced to meet National Map Accuracy Staandards (NMAS) for 1:12,000-scale products. Aerial cameras have current certification from the USGS, National Mapping Division, Optical Science Laboratory. Test calibration scans are performed on all source photography scanners. Horizontal positional accuracy is determined by the Orthophoto Accuracy (ORACC) software program for DOQ data produced by the National Mapping Division. The program determines the accuracy by finding the line and sample coordinates of the passpoints in the DOQ and fitting these to their ground coordinates to develop a root mean square error (RMSE). From 4 to 9 points are checked. As a further accuracy test, the image line and sample coordinates of the DEM corners are transformed and compared with the actual X,Y DEM corner values to determine if they are within the RMSE. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The native projection of the drawing is NM State Plane, Zone Central, NAD 83. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 10/23/2024 Tracts 101-01 and 101-02 were created from the metes and bounds as described in deeds sair01 and sair02, Tract 01-103 is based on quite a few different sources. The northwest boundary was derived from the 1942 Subdivision of Land by Arlington Homes, Inc (Plan Book 73, Plans 91 & 93), the 1943 Subdivision of Lands by Rowland Barnes (Plan 18727B) and with the 1956 Union Street Right-of-Way Land Survey (Plan Book 88, Plan 82). The north and eastern boundary is derived from the 1951 Bridge Street Survey (Plan Book 1951, Plan 346) and the 1911 Saugus Terrace Subdivision Plat (Plan Book 21, Plan 19). The southeastern boundary follows the center of the Saugus River. The source for the river boundary is 2023 Nearmap aerial photography courtesy of ESRI. The tie from the river center line to the eastern boundary of Lot 46, Saugus Terrace, is based on typical lot adjustment for river boundary movement; a line extending perpendicular to the river center line from the lot corner. The tie from the river to the east ROW of Central Street has the least amount of source information and is based on the original land status map alignment. The southwestern boundary is derived from the 1967 Survey Plan of a Portion of Central Street (Plan Book 109, Plan 61), the 1949 Subdivision of Land Owned by Donald Randazzo (Plan Book 1949, Plan 401), the 1956 Union Street Right-of-Way Land Survey (Plan Book 88, Plan 82) and the 1926 Plan of Land Owned by Welcome W. McCullough (Plan Book 46, Plan 49C). Also utilized were the descriptions included in NPS Deeds 1, 2 & 3. All of the subdivision, land plat and deed descriptions are interconnected by common surveyed points. After reconciling the different basis of bearings for each source, the entire project area was checked for final alignment utilizing the 2023 aerial photography along apparent lines of occupation, lot boundaries, road/curb alignments, and other physical boundary features that corresponded to the COGO line work. North American Datum 83(2011), Massachusetts Mainland, US Foot was used as the source coordinate system. UPDATE 09/09/2014 Tracts 101-01 and 101-02 were derived from NPS deeds sair01 and sair02. The boundary for tract 101-03 was generated from historical park legacy data and Essex County GIS data. This tract was geo-referenced to the ground from Northing’s and Easting’s referenced by survey plat, TIC number SAIR 444/41005 dated December 2003. North American Datum 83, Massachusetts Mainland, US Foot was used as the source coordinate system for the Autodesk Land desktop project. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Sequoia National Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 11/26/2008 BLM and USFS PLSS line work downloaded from the Geocommunicator (http://www.geocommunicator.gov/LSIS6/map.jsp) on 9/2/2008. This line work was used to create all aliquot part tract and boundary lines excluding those that were not included in the coverage. BLM GDBC digital flat files for T17SR33E and T15SR31E downloaded on 9/16/2008 from http://www.blm.gov/ca/st/en/prog/cadastral/gcdbpage.html since these townships were not included in the Geocommunicator coverage. All non-aliquot part tracts were created using COGO commands in AutoDesk using bearings and distances from deeds/surveys/legal descriptions. Northernmost line work for tract 05-107 transformed around the NW and SE corners of the SW of the SW of section 1 T16S R28E. Southernmost line work tract 05-107 transformed around the NW corner of the SE of the NW of section 12 and the NW corner of the SE of the SW of section 12 all in T16S R28E. Line work for tracts from segment map 02 (Oriole Lake Subdivision) were transformed between the SE corner of the SW1/4, section 8, T17SR30E (X= 6635446.68,Y= 2052273.92) and the NW corner of the SW1/4 of the Sw1/4, section 8, T17SR30E (X= 6635446.68,Y= 2052273.92) to account for ground to grid scale and rotation. The location of the NW corner for the SW1/4, section 8, T17SR30E was then moved to X= 6635408.94, Y= 2052292.89 to better align with with the 2005 NAIP imagery. Tracts from segment 07 (Silver City Forest Homes Subdivision) geo-reference using the NW coner of Section 7, T17s, R31E (x = 6663179.69, y = 2054525.29). This position was taken from BLM PLSS line-work. Tracts were rotated 0d12m21.49582s and scaled 0.999944426 around the NW coner to account for the ground to grid transformation. The refernece point for these tracts was then moved from x = 6663179.69, y = 2054525.29 to x = 6663141.20, y = 2054563.76 to align with the 2005 NAIP imagery. Where the boundary did not follow aliquot part divisions, USGS delineation of hydrographic divides was used from 1:24,000 scale DRG's. These delineations were not available for tract 06-101, so basins were created from USGS 10-meter DEM's that define the divide. California State Plane, Zone IV, NAD83, US Foot was used as the source coordinate system for the Autodesk Land Desktop project. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Sitka National Historical Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 03/21/2019 In June 1974, the SITK hand-drawn mylar Land Resources Division segment sheet was created by the Denver Service Center. From the year 2000 forward it was redrawn and revised as needed by the Alaska Lands cartographer until 2003. In 1996, the park boundary and tracts were digitized from the Sitka National Historical Park segment map by NPS-contractor GeoNorth Inc. using ESRI software in the form of coverages, and, under the direction of the GIS and Lands Teams. In 1997, all disposed tracts outside of the park boundary were dropped from the GIS. From 1999 to 2001, Encompass Mapping and Data, under contract to NPS and using ESRI software in the form of coverages, began a major update and revision process of the park boundary and tracts. Attribute and linework errors were resolved. From 2002 to 2009, boundary and tract changes were either performed by the cartographer for the Alaska Land Resources Program Center using either Autodesk or ArcGIS software, then submitted in the form of Autodesk-exported or native ArcGIS shapefiles, jpegs, and requested attribute changes to Encompass Mapping and Data; or, the data was created/edited by Encompass Mapping and Data under the direction of the Lands cartographer. Most of the changes made by the Lands cartographer consisted of moving tracts to more accurate locations, cogoing the U.S., BLM, DNR-Right of Way, NPS, and private surveys using survey and Autodesk software, and using the official documentation for the park boundary. The State DOT ROW surveys and Patrick O'Neill private survey plats were used to cogo the park boundary and tracts 01-102, 01-103, and 01-122 in 2004-2006. The Alaska State Tidelands surveys were used to cogo the park boundary and tracts 01-111 and 01-112. The park was mapped with 2 foot contours and portions of the boundary surveyed by 2-3 different private contractors using photogrammetric and topographic survey mapping techniques. Portions of the tracts/park boundary were also surveyed at that time by the same contractors in 1992/1995, then finished and revised in 2001-2003. Encompass converted the data into ArcInfo files, attributed it, and submitted the data each time to the GIS team for inclusion into the GIS Permanent Data Set (PDS). In 2008, Lands cartographers cogoed the park boundary and tracts 01-113 to 01-118 in the Russian Bishops's House area. This portion of the park was not available digitally until then. In April 2009, Encompass Mapping and Data converted all lands data from coverages into a land status and boundary geodatabase created under contract to the AKRO-GIS Team. Specifications as delineated by GIS and Lands personnel were followed. Tract and boundary data is continually updated with land status changes and ongoing improvement of linework/attribution as better source information becomes available. The tract and boundary data has all been reprojected (when needed) to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude and longitude. A major remapping effort was completed for ~90% of the native allotments and other small private parcels. They were systematically revised and/or checked for correct location and conveyance status. Most were remapped by COGOing in US Survey plats and/or legal descriptions or using BLM-COGOed data. Previous to these edits, most small tracts were digitized from the hard copy Segment Sheets.In addition, satellite and aerial photo ortho imagery were used to move the tracts to better locations when the latitude/longitude of the parcels were too approximate or unknown. New tracts have been broken out of existing tracts where a subdivision and sale has been made to a non-native person(s). Continuous minor editing has been performed on park boundaries where better orthoimagery and/or common boundary agreements with adjoining federal agencies have been agreed upon per the "Alaska Common Boundary Initiative". No acreage changes are taking place. Native corporation conveyance actions have been updated as the changes take place. This involves deleting selections in some cases to changing from selected status into conveyed status. Survey plats and notes are always used to COGO in the boundaries. All tracts outside the park boundaries have now been mapped.

description.gco:CharacterString: Steamtown National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 09/19/2025 Data reviewed and adjusted from compiled surveys, property records, and official boundary descriptions provided by the current Steamtown National Historic Site superintendent, NPS Land Resources Division records, and the Lackawanna County recorder of deeds online search engine. Coordinate geometry tools were used to map boundary descriptions when possible. All polygons mapped using the Traverse tool in ArcGIS Pro had to be rotated counterclockwise in order to match the land description to updated aerial imagery of the corresponding area. When using coordinate geometry was not an option, land boundaries were mapped using on-screen digitization of survey plats or pre-existing segment maps. Accuracy of all mapped boundaries is estimated to be relatively low, with boundary lines falling ten meters, more or less, from their true location. Maps depict the extent of all tracts and boundaries within in or of interest to Steamtown National Historic Site and all features are projected in NAD 1983 (2011) StatePlane Pennsylvania North FIPS3701 (US Feet). UPDATE 04/14/2021 Unacquired tracts outside the legislated boundary (102-01, 103-01, 103-02, 104-01, 104-02 and 104-03) were digitized and added to the tract data set. UPDATE 02/02/2011 All tracts were digitized in Data for Lackawanna county and Scranton were downloaded form their respective GIS data portals. This data was projected and imported into the stea project. Next the historic segment maps were georeferenced into the project geodatabase. After preliminary review it evident that a higher quality and more detailed dataset was needed. The park was contacted and the GIS staff provide an accurate parcel level GIS data set. These four sources we all used to help delineate and establish the park boundary and internal tracts. The coordinate system used was North American Datum 83,Pennsylvania State Plane, North Zone, US Foot. The This fully attributed GIS dataset is developed and verified to match the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and added to the national tract and boundary data sets.

description.gco:CharacterString: Theodore Roosevelt Island Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 12/24/2006 This dataset was created as part of a larger dataset for GWMP. Data was then adjusted for current shorelines and georeferenced using 0.2 meter pixel color orthophotography from the District of Columbia dated 1999, provided in coordinate system MD State Plane Meters NAD83. The difference between the deed line and current shoreline required that that deed acreage in the MDL to be corrected to reflect the accreation of land. This accreation of land is given to NPS by the authority of Public Law dated 6/4/1934. A seperate layer title "tract-legcy" in the orginial autocad displays the original deed line, as well on the segment maps. description.gco:CharacterString: Thomas Stone National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 07/28/2009 This data was input from the deeded legal description of tract 101-01 into NAD83 Maryland State Plane Zone US Foot using the COGO tools in ESRI's ArcMap. A ground to grid transformation was applied to all bearings and distances entered. A scale factor of 0.999968534 and a convergence of -00 01 06.01245 was applied. Corpscon 6.0.1 was used to determine the proper scale factor and convergence parameters to enter based on a estimated POB of N312415 E1303975. A relative error ratio of 1:742 was found when a least squares adjustment was used to force closure of the legal description. USGS DOQ data was downloaded from Microsoft's TerraServer on 20070813. This information was used to establish geo-referenced "point-of-beginning" for tract 101-01. The resulting tract shapefile was imported into AutoDesk. The entire file was rotated 8° 43' W based in the declination of the POB on 1/8/1981 as calculated from NOAA's NGDC web site. The Autodesk line work was imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. Tract 101-02 was manually digitized from the existing THST Segment Map 101. 2007 NAIP imagery was imported and the overall position of the unit was checked against it. Tract 101-02 did not align with physical features in the NAIP image that appear to run along the tract boundary. Tract 101-02 was moved to align with the NAIP image however the original geomerty digitized from the existing THST Segment Map 101 was not altered. The entire unit was created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layout representing the segment map was created. The tract and boundary data was then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Tuskegee Institute National Historic Site Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 01/14/2016 Tracts 101-01 (101-09), 101-02, 101-03, 101-05, 101-06, 101-07, and 101-08 were cogo'ed from legal descriptions found in their respective deeds. These legal descriptions utilized PLSS section corners for ground control. PLSS linework was downloaded from the BLM and imported into Civil3D. High resolution imagery was downloaded in the form of 30 tiles from Arc Map and mosaiced into one raster file. This raster file was also imported into Civil3D. The accuracy of the cogo'ed tracts was very poor due to un-reliable PLSS in the area. No other ground control could be obtained at this time, and so cogo'ed tracts were aligned with the high resolution imagery utilizing road edges, subdivision lines, and other features visible in the imagery. If and when updated ground control can be obtained, a new dataset will be produced. The boundary for tract 101-04 and the historic district boundary were on-screen-digitized utilizing a georeferenced version of map NHS-TI-20,000-C dates September, 1973. NAD83 Alabama State Planes, East Zone, US Foot was used as the source coordinate system for the Autodesk Civil3D project. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. description.gco:CharacterString: Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 12/24/2015 Information contained in LRD's land ownership databases is updated nightly however tract polygons are posted to the NPS Data Store on a monthly basis. Users can ensure parcel polygons have up to date ownership attribution after the publication date by contacting your regional LRD office or downloading the Current_Tract_Ownership_Data file located on the NPS Data Store (http://science.nature.nps.gov/nrdata/) in a dBase format. Please contact the data originator with any suggested corrections and updates. LRD's boundary polygons represent the current legislated boundary of a given NPS unit. NPS does not necessarily have full fee ownership or hold another interest (easement, right of way, etc...) in all parcels contained within this boundary. Equivalently NPS may own or have an interest in parcels outside the legislated boundary of a given unit. In order to obtain complete information about current NPS interests both inside and outside the units legislated boundary, LRD's tracts files should also be downloaded and used in conjunction with LRD's boundary files. Downloaded the historical USGS source maps identified above and evaluated the quality of their georeferencing by inspecting alignment of coordinates with printed grid lines on the digital maps. All source digital data were found to have mapped latitudes and longitudes that were within 0.1 seconds of the graticule coordinates printed on the map collars. Georeferenced each spliced section of the River Management Plan maps to their corresponding HTMC map using ArcGIS for Desktop software and an adjust transformation that minimizes local and global alignment errors. Used at least 100 control points per spliced section based on well-distributed, readily identifiable features until a zero error was reported for the adjust transformation. Spliced sections were rectified to the coordinate system of the source HTMC map. Evaluated discrepancies between the location of the boundary on overlapping sections of the georeferenced 1986 Upper Delaware Scenic & Recreational River Management Plan maps. Areas of discrepancies were handled as follows: • Page 1-2 south/west overlap areas: The page 1 boundary was followed through the overlap area. At the western edge of page 2, the trajectory of the page 1 boundary was continued due east approximately 27 meters until it met with the page 2 boundary at 75°11’7.334’’W, 41°51’7.738’’N. This resulted in exclusion of an approximately 52 meter stretch of the page 2 boundary that did not coincide with the trajectory of the page 1 boundary. The boundary as drawn on the georeferenced sections from the 1986 Upper Delaware Scenic & Recreational River Management Plan was digitized with the map display set to 1:24,000. In accordance with the Superintendent's decision, the outside of the boundary line was followed during digitization and the overlap areas were handled as outlined above. The coordinate system of the boundary vector layer was set to that of the Page 4 N section, which is nearest the geometric center of the boundary. The interior tracts were created through a combination of deeds, surveys, legal descriptions, as well as on-screen digitization. Tracts that did not have any deed, legal, or survey were on-screen digitized from the previous set of UPDE segment maps. Smaller scale maps have a larger level of inaccuracy. It is assumed that the boundary and tract information meets National Map Accuracy Standards and should be considered no better than the listed sources. The Autodesk line work is imported, edited, attributed, approved, and a link and node topology is developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step.

description.gco:CharacterString: Valles Caldera National Preserve Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 06/10/2025 Geometry for tract 101-10 updated based on recorded survey completed by Kurt A. Luebke, PLS 25337 titled Boundary Line Adjustment Survey on March 1, 2024 (Reception No. 2024P02278, 8/16/2024) in Sandoval County. UPDATE 03/05/2025 Geometry for tracts 101-08 and 101-09 updated based on recorded survey completed by Kurt A. Luebke, PLS 25337 titled Boundary Line Adjustment Survey on March 1, 2024 (Reception No. 2024P02278, 8/16/2024) in Sandoval County. UPDATE 03/13/2024 Minor updates near boundary with BAND where coincident as BAND was adjusted based on current BLM surveys. In addition, tract 101-03 came into the boundary once acquired per Solicitor opinion received January 27, 2020 and correspondence in email from February 9, 2022. Tracts 101-08 and 101-09 revised based on Boundary Line Adjustment Survey by Kurt. A. Luebke, PS 25337; Survey will be certified and recorded in the near future. UPDATE 09/12/2022 Geometry for tract 101-08 was updated and tract 101-09 was created based on surveys completed by Edward M. Doak, N.M.P.L.S. No. 8127 on May 5, 2005 (Reception No. 200516063), on May 7, 2010 (Reception No. 2010P00190), and on July 29, 2021 (reception No. 2021P01725). All land survey plats are filed with the Sandoval County Clerk and Recorder's Office in Bernalillo, New Mexico. NPS completed a field investigation on 08/26/2022 to verify survey corner monuments set during the Doak and prior surveys. Parcel location is based on a grant boundary adjustment between found monuments set in 1983. New land survey to reset lost monumentation is being ordered. UPDATE 04/06/2021 Created new tract 101-08 for potential acquisition at Jemez Springs HQ. Legal descriptions and polygons are preliminary and WILL change based on land survey, once completed. Land survey will supersede all preliminary information. Survey record utilized for this update dated back to 1978 while utilizing a survey completed in 2010 with significant misclosure. UPDATE 03/07/2019 Merged tracts 101-03, 04, 05, 06 & 07 into one tract called 101-03 under a new owner's name. UPDATE 04/06/2016 Creation: Created an ArcGIS geodatabase project in New Mexico State Plane Coordinates, Central Zone, NAD 83, US Survey Foot projection. CadNSDI v2 data was downloaded from the New Mexico RGIS website. Published corner accuracies range from +/-27 feet to +/-89 feet. Due to the high error factor, other sources were used to spatially anchor the tract and boundary file. For the northeast corner, a 2002 Land Survey Plat cites NM SP coords for the Point of Commencement as X:1,600,622.44, Y:1,821,962.49 (NMSP CZ 83). The north boundary of the Baca Location No. 1 was adjusted to this published point. Mile Marker #4 on the west boundary as surveyed with cited coordinates of X:1,530,399.76, Y:1,777,824.59 (NMSP CZ 83). The west boundary of the Baca Location No. 1 was adjusted to this point. The southeast corner is located from NM SR 4 plan set as part of the Bandelier N.M. conversion process. The east boundary of the Baca Location No. 1 was adjusted between the 2002 survey plat and NM SR 4 location. The center line of NM SR 4 was entered and adjusted to 2014 NAIP imagery for best fit location as another anchor source. The south boundary was adjusted the Elk Meadows Subdivision, the DT Morrison Land Survey plat and NM SR 4. A local copy of the CadNSDI was spatial adjusted to the boundary for final map production. Tract and boundary data layers developed according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5.

description.gco:CharacterString: Valley Forge National Historical Park Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 09/24/2025 Update to the entire tract and boundary data utilizing an AutoCAD file provided as a deliverable for a 2011 boundary survey for NPS prepared by Thomas R. Badenoch, PLS SU-042314-R on behalf of The RBA Group, NPS TIC Map No. 464-100675. NPS deed descriptions and recorded survey documents in Montgomery and Chester Counties were utilized to fill in private inholding boundaries or external boundaries identified after 2011. UPDATE 05/01/2018 The VAFO Land Status Map (Segment 101) was scanned and saved as a tagged image format file (.tiff). The scanned image was georeferenced to the VAFO orthophoto mosaic using ArcGIS 8.3. The georeferenced image was edited, using the ArcGIS 8.3 Raster Painting tools, to remove extraneous lines and fill in gaps in tract boundary lines. The edited image was vectorized using the ArcGIS 8.3 ArcScan tools to produce a line shapefile. The line shapefile was manually edited to delete extraneous nodes, reshape arcs, etc., using the VAFO orthophoto mosaic as a guide. Scanned images of each inset map, Inset A (Segment 101), Inset B (Segment 101), and Inset C (Segment 102), were georeferenced to the main map shapefile, using ArcGIS 8.3, resulting in three separate inset shapefiles. Each inset shapefile was rubbersheeted to the main map shapefile using ArcGIS 8.3 Spatial Adjustment tools. The rubbersheeted, Inset A shapefile was merged with the main map shapefile using ArcGIS 8.3. The merged shapefile was converted to an ArcInfo line coverage and topology was cleaned using ArcInfo 8.3. The cleaned coverage was converted to a shapefile and duplicate/coincident lines that were not eliminated in the topology cleaning process were manually deleted. Identical procedures were used to merge the Inset B and C shapefiles with the main map shapefile. (After each merge, the resulting shapefile was converted to a coverage, cleaned, converted back to a shapefile, and manually edited, as described above.) The final, merged shapefile was rubbersheeted to the VAFO orthophoto mosaic using ArcGIS 8.3 Spatial Adjustment tools. A minor boundary revision was passed in 2012 which brought in tracts 101-79 and 101-80. These 2 tracts were created using coordinate geometry from a survey included in a document describing the transfer of these two right of ways to the park, titeld "Transmittal of the Proposed Boundary Descriptions for the Right-of-Way and Structure Donations to the National Park Service", dated March 3, 2017.

description.gco:CharacterString: Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument Tract and Boundary Data UPDATE 04/04/2013 Line work was provided in a shapefile format by Minerals Management Service (MMS), Mapping and Boundary Branch, located in Lakewood CO. This data is part of a larger project known as Technical Information Management System (TIMS), Mapping System, Block and Boundary Component . The shapefile was imported into AutoCAD from UTM zone 20 to NAD83 Puerto Rico and Virgin Islands, US Foot. Data was clean, accurate, and verified using NAIP One Meter Ortho Imagery (Natural Color), dated 2004-Present. The original process for the data development is described in a Process Step of this metadata file and provided by MMS. No edits or adjustments were made. Attributes were assigned in Autodesk using object data. Line work was developed both for the tract and boundary data layers according to the procedures described in the Land Acquisition Procedures Manual Chapter 5. The entire unit is created in a geographically contiguous model space and separate layouts representing each individual segment map are created. The tract and boundary data is then reprojected to North American Datum 1983 generic latitude & longitude and exported from Autodesk to an ArcView shape file format in a single step. UPDATE 01/01/2002 Process Described by MMI: Baseline points from the nautical charts and MMS GPS surveys were used to project the 3 mile line and equidistant lines (using in-house TIMS computer programs). These lines were appended with the International boundary, previous NPS offshore park boundaries and (in Coral Bay) the NOAA coastline file. Unneeded lines were then removed and the coverage was cleaned in Arc/Info to build topology. **Abstract: This dataset contains the boundary lines for the Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument created by Presidential Proclamation 7399, January 17, 2001 as recorded in the Federal Register/ Vol. 66, No. 14/ Monday, January 22, 2001/Presidential Documents p. 7364-7367 frwebgate.access.gpo.gov/cgi- bin/getdoc.cgi?dbname=2001_presidential_documents&docid=pd22ja01_txt-31. The Monument consists of 5 distinct units, deemed to be on Federal Submerged Lands. These five parcels are bounded by: existing offshore Park boundaries, shoreline, International Treaty lines, the 3 nautical mile Territorial Submerged Lands Act Boundary, and equidistant lines subdividing Federal and Territorial submerged lands. The Territorial Submerged Lands Act, October 5, 1974 www4.law.cornell.edu/uscode/48/1705.html conveyed submerged lands inside a 3 nautical mile line to the territories. However all submerged lands adjacent to property owned by the United States above the line of mean high tide were excepted from that transfer. A land title search was conducted to determine which coastal properties were owned by the United States at the time of the act (October 5, 1974). MMS then used in-house programs contained in their Technical Information Management System (TIMS) to project equidistant lines between Territorial and US lands, seaward to the 3 nautical mile line. The 3 nautical mile line was computed by TIMS after picking baselines from the most current NOAA nautical charts and field checking questionable "asterisk rocks". Coordinates for the existing offshore Park boundaries were obtained from the Park Service. Shoreline for Hurricane Hole/Coral Bay, were obtained from a vector conversion of NOAA shoreline T-Sheets (1:40,000 scale) available from www.csc.noaa.gov/products/shorelines/digdata.htm . Coordinates for the US-UK treaty line were taken from the treaty available from www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/PDFFILES/TREATIES/GBR- USA1993MB.PDF. The file consists of 5 polygons for the 5 distinct areas of the park, however the unit in Coral Bay also has several tiny ( 0 acre ) polygons representing many tiny islands within Coral Bay unit. Because GIS projection and topology functions can change or generalize coordinates, these GIS files are NOT an official record for exact park boundaries. For precise coordinates see the OPD and SOBD diagrams. **Purpose: This line shows the boundary for the new Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument as created by Presidential Proclamation 7399. Cadastre data the MMS produces is generated in accordance with ownership and mineral resource management. **Supplemental_Information: Some confusion may have been generated by the map which was included with the Proclamation (see: Federal Register/ Vol. 66, No. 14/ Monday, January 22, 2001/Presidential Documents p. 7367). That map shows cross hatching extending over 2 parcels of Territorial Submerged Lands (83.863260 Ac. and 1100.814245 Ac.). However the Proclamation specified (middle of p. 7365) that the Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument only covered "lands owned or controlled by the United States" consisting of approximately 12,708 marine acres. Please see the revised map included with this metadata, VIMon.pdf. Additional information on the technical procedures used by MMS to determine offshore boundaries can be found in OCS Report MMS 99-0006: Boundary Development on the Outer Continental Shelf, available from www.mms.gov/itd/pubs/1999/99-0006.PDF Also see GAO document B-287626, regarding Ownership and Control of U.S. Virgin Islands Monument Lands, released November 15, 2002, available from http://www.gao.gov/.
